Megy este a legény haza, bétereli a száz nyulat a nagy kapun.
Hát jő eleibe a király, káromkodik, hogy reng belé az udvar.
- Jere csak, jere, te kötélrevaló, mit küldöttél te nekem a zsákba!
Feleli a legény:
- Az Isten Istenem ne legyen, ha nem nyulat, felséges királyom.
Hívják a szolgálót.
- Hát mit adott neked a pásztor, te leány?
- Nekem bizony, felséges királyom,
életem-halálom a kezedbe ajánlom, igazán nyulat adott.
- Hm - mondja a király -,
még ilyent sem ettem világi életemben, hát most már hol a nyúl?
Számlálják a nyulakat, egyszer, kétszer, háromszor, de csak mindig száz jött ki.
- No, hallod-e, te szegény legény - mondá a király -,
még ilyen pásztorom sem volt, hogy küldjön is nyulat, s ne is hiányozzék.
Hát mit kívánsz?
- Csak egy kád pénzt, felséges királyom, mert nagy a szegénység otthon.
A király tüstént méretett egy istenes nagy zsák pénzt,
hogy a legény tizenkét ökörrel húzatta haza.
De bezzeg olyan erősen meggazdagodtak, hogy csudájára jártak messze földről.
Ma is élnek, ha meg nem haltak.
Az acélgyűrű
Hol volt, hol nem volt, volt egyszer egy szegény ember.
Ez a szegény ember elment egyszer az erdőbe fáért.
Amint a száraz ágakat szedegetné, felvesz az ágakkal egy kígyófiút.
Meg akarja ölni, de a kígyófiú megszólal, s azt mondja neki:
- Ne ölj meg, te szegény ember,
mert egész életedre boldoggá teszlek, ha meghagyod az életemet.
- Ugyan, mit beszélsz, te kígyófiú - mondá a szegény ember -,
nem vagyok én olyan bugyuta bolond, hogy higgyek a te ígéretednek.
- Már bizony csak higgy nekem, szegény ember, s nem bánod meg.
Nesze, adok neked egy acélgyűrűt, húzd fel az ujjadra,
s ha valami kívánságod lesz az életben,
csak fordítsd meg az ujjadon ezt a gyűrűt,
én mindjárt ott termek, s teljesítem a kívánságodat.
"Isten neki - gondolá a szegény ember -, ha nem használ,
nem is árt." Elfogadá a gyűrűt, felhúzá az ujjára, s azzal elment haza.
Még jóformán meg sem állapodott otthon,
megfordítja az ujján a gyűrűt, s hát ott terem a kicsi kígyó.
- Mit parancsolsz, édes gazdám?
- Azt parancsolom - mondja a szegény ember -,
hogy holnap reggelre nekem olyan palotát teremts ide,
amilyen még a török császárnak sincs.
- Meglesz, édes gazdám - mondá a kicsi kígyó,
s csak eltűnt, mintha a föld nyelte volna el.
No, lefekszik este a szegény ember, alszik, mint a bunda.
Hát mikor reggel felébredt, szeme-szája tátva maradt,
olyan fényes palota kerekedett a rongyos házikója helyébe.
Olyan volt ez, amilyent emberi szem még nem látott e világi életben!
Csupa színarany volt körülötte minden, de minden.
Még az asztal is arany volt,
s annak a közepén akkora tál színaranyból, mint egy taligakerék.
"No - mondja magában a szegény ember -, mégsem csala meg az a kicsi kígyó.
Ejnye, de okosan tettem, hogy meghagytam az életét!"
Ismét fordít egyet a gyűrűn, s a kicsi kígyó abban a percben ott termett.
- Mit parancsolsz, édes gazdám?
- Azt parancsolom, hogy hozd el nekem feleségül a fekete király leányát.
- Meglesz, édes gazdám!
Hát Krisztus úgy segéljen,
másnap reggel csakugyan ott volt vele egy szobában a fekete király leánya.
De aztán halljátok, olyan gyönyörűséges szép leány volt ez,
hogy a napra lehetett nézni, de arra nem.
Hej, boldog volt a szegény ember, úgy élt, mint egy császár.
Mindent kapott, amit szeme-szája kívánt,
csak egyet kellett csavarintania azon az acélgyűrűn,
ott termett a kicsi kígyó, meghozott mindent.
Sok-sok idő járt le, mikor a szegény ember kimozdult egyszer abból a gyönyörű palotából.
Elment hazulról, s otthon felejtette az acélgyűrűt.
Éppen a palota előtt megy el egy vén ószeres, s torkaszakadtából kiabálja:
- Gyűrűt vegyenek!
Gyűrűt!
Kitekint az asszony, behívja,
s a boldogtalan odaadja az acélgyűrűt egy aranygyűrűért, még rá is fizet.
De hogy, hogy nem, az ószeres tudta az acélgyűrű titkát,
s amint kikerült az utcára, mindjárt fordított egyet rajta.
Abban a pillanatban ott termett a kicsi kígyó.
Kérdi:
- Mit parancsolsz, édes gazdám?
- Azt parancsolom, hogy ezt a palotát vedd fel asszonyostul,
mindenestül, s vidd el az Óperenciás-tenger túlsó partjára.
- Meglesz, édes gazdám!
Hát édes jó Istenem, mire a szegény ember hazavetődött,
csak a puszta helye maradt annak a drága, szép, fényes palotának!
Aj! elbúsulja magát, s nagy szomorúan világgá indul,
hátha valahol megtalálná a palotáját.
Ment, mendegélt hegyen-völgyön által, hetedhét ország ellen.
Amint az Óperenciás-tenger innenső szélére érne,
meglát egy kutyát, aki döglőfélben hentergett a tenger partján.
Keservesen nyöszörgött, vinnyogott, s szörnyű kauszolással kérte a szegény embert,
hogy gyógyítsa meg, ne hagyja ott veszni.
A szegény ember mindenféle jó füvet szedegetett,
azokkal meggyógyította, s ketten továbbmentek.
Hát alig mennek egy jó puskalövésnyire, egy beteg macskát találnak.
Ez is kéri a szegény embert, hogy gyógyítsa meg.
Jól van, meggyógyítja, s most már hárman mennek tovább.
Mennek, mendegélnek a tenger partján, s egyszer csak nagyot kiált a szegény ember:
- Ne, te, né!
Az én palotám ott van a túlsó parton.
No, ezt jól elköltözteté valaki!
Hej!
Hej!
Uram, Jézus Krisztus, ha valami csudálatos módon keresztüljuthatnék,
nem adnám egy csikós kancáért.
Azt mondja a kutya:
- Ne búsulj, te szegény ember!
Jót tettél velem, jótétel helyébe jót várj.
Általúszok én a tengeren, s majdcsak kieszelek valamit.
A macska is mondja, hogy bizony ő is átmegy a kutyával, ha addig él is,
s a szemit bé sem hunyja, míg a palota vissza nem kerekedik a régi helyére.
Nem is készülődnek sokáig, hanem a kutya csak nagy hirtelen a tengerbe ugrik,
utána a macska, felül a kutya hátára, s úgy úsznak által.
De hogy szómat össze ne keverjem, a szegény ember jól szájába rágta a kutyának is,
a macskának is, hogy abban a palotában egy acélgyűrűnek kell lenni.
Azt mindenképpen kerítsék meg, egyébre ügyet se vessenek.
Ha azt a gyűrűt megkapták, csak siessenek vissza, a többi az ő gondja.
Átalúsznak, s bémennek a palotába.
Hát ott alszik éppen az ószeres, s a gyűrű fel van kötve a szakállára.
Hiszen a macskának sem kellett egyéb.
Odalopózkodik az ágyhoz, szépen leoldja a gyűrűt, s azzal uzsgyi neki,
vesd el magad! kiszaladtak a palotából,
belé a tengerbe, s úsztak visszafelé nagy szaporán.
De mikor éppen a tenger kellős közepire értek volna - csak hallgassátok meg,
hogy mit csinált az a szerencsétlen "macskabéka" macska!
-, arra úszik egy hal, a macska utánakap, s a gyűrűt a tengerbe ejti.
Hé, fikon teremtette, volt nemulass!
A kutya a tengerbe akarta nyuvasztani az oktalan macskát,
de addig rimánkolódott, hogy mégis megkegyelmezett az életinek.
No, már most mit csináljanak, merre facsarodjanak?
Búcsálódnak szörnyűségesen, nem mertek visszaúszni a gyűrű nélkül.
Meg kell azt keríteni, ha a föld fenekéből is.
Amint így búcsálódnak, a macska elkap egy halat.
Hát ez éppen a halak királyának volt a fia!
Könyörög a halacska:
- Ne ölj meg, édes macskám, én a halkirály fia vagyok,
nem bánod meg, ha meghagyod az életemet!
Elmennek vele a halak királyához, s elmondják annak, hogy így s így jártak.
Ők megkegyelmeztek a fia életének, kerítse meg azt a gyűrűt,
mert bizonyosan valamelyik hal nyelte el.
A halak királya mindjárt országgyűlést hívott, s kikérdezett minden halat,
hogy nincs-e gyűrű nála, de mindenik csak azt felelte,
hogy még a nemzetségének sem volt gyűrűje.
Erőst megszomorodik a kutya, de még a macska is,
s már éppen indulóban voltak, mikor jelentik, hogy egy hal még oda van.
Várnak egy kicsit, hátha annál van a gyűrű.
Csakugyan jő is nagy megizzadva egy "sánta" hal, s hát hozza a gyűrűt!
Aj, megörvend a kutya, de még a macska is,
el akarja kapni a gyűrűt, de a kutya nagyot mordul:
- Hagyd el hé, nem bízom reád többet!
Te csak kucorodj a hátamra, én veszem a gyűrűt a szájamba!
Még "j' egésséget" sem mondottak, úgy elszaladtak.
Kiúsznak a partra, s átaladják a gyűrűt a szegény embernek.
Egyszeribe felhúzza az ujjára, csavarint egyet, s a kicsi kígyó mindjárt ott terem.
- Mit parancsolsz, édes gazdám?
- Azt parancsolom - mondá a szegény ember -,
hogy azt a házat vidd vissza a régi helyire, az ószerest pedig felejtsd a túlsó parton.
- Meglesz, édes gazdám.
Úgy is lett, ahogy a szegény ember parancsolta.
A szép palota visszakerült asszonyostul, mindenestül oda,
ahol legelőször volt, s a szegény ember ismét boldogul élt.
A kutyáról s a macskáról sem feledkezett meg:
tejbe-vajba fürösztötte, s hasábfával kenegette őket.
Az igaz, hogy ezek azótától fogvást haragusznak egymásra,
de mégis élnek, ha meg nem haltak.
A halász és a felesége
Volt egyszer egy halász s annak felesége.
Egy kicsi putriban laktak, a tenger partján,
s bizony nagy szegénységben éltek, mert mikor került horogra hal, mikor nem.
Hát egyszer mi történt?
Az történt, hogy egy szörnyű nagy cápa akadt a halász horgára.
Húzza, húzza a halász, de a hal megszólal:
- Hagyd meg az életemet, nem vagyok én hal, hanem elátkozott királyfi.
Ugyan mit érnél velem, ha kifognál?
Úgy sem ehetnéd meg a húsomat.
- Igazad van, mondotta a halász, eredj Isten hírével, ha csakugyan nem vagy igazi hal.
Eleresztette a halat s hazament üres tarisznyával.
- Hallá-e, hát megint nem fogott halat?
- kérdezte az asszony.
- Mi lesz velünk?
- Dehogy nem fogtam, mondotta a halász,
fogtam egy szörnyű nagy cápát, de nem volt igazi hal.
Azt mondta, hogy elátkozott királyfi, s addig kért, hogy eleresztettem.
- No azt elég rosszúl cselekedte.
Addig legalább ne eresztette volna el, míg valami kivánságát nem teljesíti.
- Ugyan bizony mit kivántam volna tőle?
- Hát azt, hogy e helyett a nyomorúságos putri helyett építsen nekünk egy tisztességes házat.
Menjen csak kend vissza, s ha még egyszer a horgára akad,
el ne eressze, míg a házat meg nem igéri.
A halász csak csóválta a fejét, gondolta, hogy az ugyan hiábavaló kivánság,
de visszament a tenger partjára, s elkezdett kiabálni:
Itt vagy-e, itt vagy-e,
Elátkozott királyfi?
Hallod-e, hallod-e,
A tengerből szállj ki.
Abban a pillanatban nagyot csobbant,
loccsant a tenger, kibukkant a hal s kérdezte a halászt:
Mit akarsz, vén halász?
Felelt a halász:
A putrinál jobb a ház.
Feleségem kivánsága:
Putri helyett legyen háza.
Mondotta a hal:
Eredj haza, vén halász,
Meg lesz reggelre a ház.
Hát csakugyan reggelre megvolt a szép kis kőház, ebben ébredtek fel.
- No lássa-e kend, mondotta az asszony, csak kivánni kell valamit s teljesül.
Most menjen vissza, s mondja neki, hogy szép kis kőház,
szép, szép, de szűk nekünk, építsen helyette palotát.
- Ó, asszony, asszony, mit gondolsz.
Elég nagy nekünk ez a ház.
Mit csinálnál a palotában?
- Arra ne legyen gondja kendnek, csak menjen s kérjen palotát!
- Megharagszik a hal, asszony, ne bolondozz!
- Haragszik, nem haragszik, csak mondja kend, amit én mondok.
Holnap reggelre palota legyen itt, de olyan, hogy a királynak se különb.
Mit volt mit tenni, elment a halász, szólította a halat:
Itt vagy-e, itt vagy-e,
Elátkozott királyfi?
Hallod-e, hallod-e,
A tengerből szállj ki.
Jött a hal azonnal s kérdezte:
Mit akarsz, te vén halász?
Felelt a halász:
Kicsi nekünk az a ház.
Feleségem azt kivánja:
Legyen neki palotája.
Mondotta a hal:
Hát csak eredj haza szépen,
Reggel a palota készen.
Haza megy a halász, lefekszenek, s ím' reggel egy akkora palotában ébredtek fel,
hogy volt annak hetvenhét szobája,
a szobákban arany lócák, asztalok, ágyak, földig érő tükrök.
Még az ablak is színarany volt, az a garádicsa is.
Mindenfelé inasok, szolgálók sürögtek, forogtak;
a palotától nem messze volt egy rengeteg nagy istálló, abban aranyszőrü paripák:
éppen mikor beléptek oda, a halász meg a halászné,
akkor vakarták a lovászok arany vakaróval, kefélték arany kefével.
- No, mondta az asszony, ugy-e jó volt, hogy palotát kívántam.
- Jó, jó, mondta a halász, ennél már egyebet nem is kivánhatsz.
- Hát arról még gondolkozom, mondta az asszony.
Másnap reggel azt mondja az asszony:
- Hiszen szép ez a palota, szép, de akkor lenne csak igazán szép, ha király volnék.
Menjen kend a halhoz s mondja meg neki, hogy király akarok lenni.
- Asszony, asszony, mit beszélsz?
Meg sem merem azt mondani!
- Mért ne merné?
Csak menjen kend, mondja meg bátran, hogy király akarok lenni.
Elment a halász nagy búsan, mert sehogy sem tetszett neki az asszony dolga.
Most már bizonyosan megharagszik az elátkozott királyfi, hogyne haragudnék meg!
Az ám, a tenger színe sem volt tiszta, mint máskor, szűrke volt,
piszkos volt, mintha az is haragudnék s zúgott, morgott erősen.
Hanem a feleségétől még jobban félt, mint a tengertől, jobban,
mint az elátkozott királyfitól s szólította, mint máskor:
Itt vagy-e, itt vagy-e,
Elátkozott királyfi?
Hallod-e, hallod-e,
A tengerből szállj ki!
Nagyot loccsant, nagyot csobbant a tenger víze, a hal kibukkant, s kérdezte a halászt:
Mi baj, mi baj vén halász?
Tán nem elég nagy a ház?
Felelt a halász:
Jaj dehogy nem, baj sincs semmi, semmi,
Csak az asszony király akar lenni!
Mondta a hal:
Ha csak ez a kivánsága,
Meg lesz ám a királysága!
Hát, Uram Jézus, mire hazaért a halász, a palota megnagyobbodott,
meg az udvar is, a palota előtt strázsák állottak,
az udvaron generálisok sétáltak fel s alá,
zengett a katonabanda muzsikája, maséroztak a katonák,
jobbra, balra kanyarodtak,
a halászné meg fent űlt a palota legnagyobb termében, színarany trónszéken,
előtte állottak a strázsák, jöttek, mentek,
szaladgáltak, hajladoztak előtte az udvari népek.
- Ó Jézusom, csapta össze kezét a halász, hát csakugyan király lett belőled?
- Király bizony, mondotta az asszony.
Talán bizony nem lát kend.
Ihol fejemen a korona.
- Na ez igazán szép dolog.
Ezzel megelégedhetel halálod órájáig.
- Bezzeg, hogy kend megelégednék, de én nem.
Mindjárt takarodjék vissza a halhoz, s mondja neki, hogy pápa akarok lenni.
- Ó asszony, asszony, mit beszélsz.
Pápa csak egy van az egész világon, az nem lehetsz.
- Egy szót se többet, rikkantott az asszony,
takarodjék kend, mert mindjárt fejét vétetem!
De még a hideg is kirázta a szegény halászt erre a szörnyű nagy kivánságra.
De hiába, mégis csak ment a tenger partjára, szólt a halnak:
Itt vagy-e, itt vagy-e,
Elátkozott királyfi?
Hallod-e, hallod-e,
A tengerből szállj ki.
Haj, de a tenger zavaros volt, olyan zavaros, s úgy zúgott,
mormogott, hogy a szegény halász szemét, fülét befogta ijedtében.
Aztán egyszerre csak felvetette magát a hal, látszott rajta, hogy már ő is haragszik.
Rákiáltott a halászra:
No, mit akarsz, jer elébb,
A királyság sem elég?
Felelt a halász:
Jaj, nem elég, nem elég,
Most pápaság kellenék!
Csak pápaság?
- szólt a cápa,
Isten neki, legyen pápa!
Szalad haza a halász nagy örömmel,
s hát a királyi palota mellett egy akkora templom van, hogy a tornyai - volt vagy ezer!
- majd az eget verték, bemegy oda s hát ott űl az asszony a trónján,
osztja az áldást nagy kegyesen a népeknek, s aki csak odafér, csókolja a lábát.
Az ám, odavergődik a halász is, térdre esik,
s a felesége lábát csókolja s mondja e közben:
- No feleség, most már pápa is lettél,
ennél több nem lehetsz, de ezzel csakugyan meg is elégedhetel.
- Majd meglátjuk, mondotta az asszony.
Egész éjjel nem aludt, folyton hánykolódott,
s mind azon gondolkozott, hogy mi lehetne még belőle.
- Hopp, megvan!
- kiáltott fel az asszony.
- Isten lesz belőlem.
Felköltötte az urát s mondta neki, hogy szaladjon izibe a halhoz,
adja elé a kivánságát: Isten akar lenni, nem elég neki a pápaság.
- Asszony, asszony, te megháborodtál az elmédben, mit gondoltál?
- Azt, amit, menjen kend szaporán.
Haj, édes jó Istenem, kétszer is kirázta a hideg a szegény halászt, míg a tengerhez ért.
Hát még mikor meglátta a tengert!
Mert volt ahogy volt eddig, de most a tenger úgy zúgott, bőgött,
kavargott, hánykolódott, mintha az egész világot el akarta volna nyelni.
A szegény halász csak állott egy helyben, de ki sem merte nyítani a száját.
De jött a hal, nem várta a kérdést, ő maga kérdezte szörnyű haragosan:
A pápaság sem elég?
Ugyan még mi kellenék?
Felelt a halász reszketve, fogvacogva:
Ó jaj, mit tudjak tenni,
Most Isten akar lenni!
Hej, szörnyü haragra gerjedt az elátkozott királyfi,
szikrát hányt a szeme s akkorát ordított, hogy a szegény halász hanyatt esett ijedtében.
Mit akar a vén liba?
Mars vissza a putriba!
Abban a pillanatban a tenger elborított mindent, de mindent,
s másnap reggel, mikor ismét vissza szállott a medrébe,
nem volt egyéb a tenger partján, csak a kis putri,
ott űlt előtte a halász, meg a halászné nagy búsan, éppen mint régen.
Még ma is élnek, ha meg nem haltak.
A szerencsés János
Volt egyszer egy legény, János volt a neve.
Ez a János hét teljes esztendeig lakott egy gazdánál,
s mikor a hetedik esztendő kitelt, azt mondta a gazdájának:
- Gazduram, kitelt az időm, most már hazamék az édes anyámhoz: fizesse ki a béremet.
- Jól van, János, mondotta a gazda,
derék legény voltál, becsületesen szógáltál, itt a béred.
Adott neki egy akkora darab aranyat,
mint a János feje, még annál is valamivel nagyobbat,
azt János belekötötte egy zacskóba, felvette a vállára s elindúlt hazafelé.
Amint ment, mendegélt, szembe jön vele egy lovasember s János elkezdett sóhajtozni:
- Hej, Istenem, de szép dolog a lovaglás.
A lovasember úgy űl a lovon, akár a széken, nem botorkázik a kőben,
a csizmáját sem szaggatja s mégis halad előre.
Hallotta ezt a lovasember s mondja Jánosnak:
- Hát aztán mért jársz gyalog?
- Azért, mondta János, mert nincs lovam.
Ezt az aranyat pedig haza kell vinnem - hét esztendőt szolgáltam érte!
Hej, pedig de nehéz, majd leszakad a vállam.
Tudod mit?
Cseréljünk, mondotta a lovasember.
Én neked adom a lovat, te meg add nekem az aranyat.
- Jó szívvel, mondotta János s abban a pillanatban levetette válláról a zsákot.
A lovasember leszállott a lóról, Jánost fölsegítette rá s még jó tanáccsal is ellátta:
- Aztán ha gyorsan akarsz haladni, akkor csak bíztasd:
nye, te, nye! s úgy szalad, mint a sebes szél.
Na, Istennek ajánlották egymást, elváltak, ketten mentek kétfelé.
Hej, hogy örűlt János!
Most már van lova.
De milyen lova!
Megrántotta a kantárszárat, bíztatta a lovat: nye,
te, nye! s a ló csakugyan neki is iramodott, de úgy,
hogy János egyszer balra, másszor jobbra billent s addig billent erre,
arra, míg egyszer csak - supp! belefordúlt az árokba.
Alig tudott szegény feje feltápászkodni, a csontja is ropogott,
fájt minden tagja s ugyancsak megbánta, hogy lóra cserélte az aranyat.
Éppen mikor feltápászkodott, jött arra felé egy ember, ki tehenet hajtott.
Ez az ember megfogta a lovat s kérdezte Jánost:
- Mi baj, öcsém?
Levetett a ló, úgy-e?
- Jaj, le, hogy a farkasok ették volna meg.
No de nem is ülök többet erre a dögre.
Hej, csak jobb a tehén a lónál!
Az ember szép csendesen ballag utána s amellett még tejet is ad, vajat is ad.
- Tudod, mit, szólt a paraszt, cseréljünk.
- Jó szívvel, mondotta János.
Szakadjon meg a kend nyaka, ne az enyém!
- Ne félj te attól, mondotta a paraszt,
s azzal felpattant a lóra s úgy elvágtatott, mint a sebes szél.
János is elindúlt a tehénnel, szép csendesen eregéltek.
Hej, Istenem, de boldog volt János!
Most már egész életében nem lesz gondja.
Csak kenyere legyen, lesz hozzá tej is, vaj is, ha akarja, sajt is: mi kell még, János?
Útközben betért egy korcsmába, ott a mi kenyér volt vele,
megette, volt egy pár garasa, ivott bort is,
aztán virágos kedvvel megint felkerekedett s mentek ketten,
mendegéltek, szép csendesen eregéltek hazafelé.
Délre járt az idő, rekkenő meleg volt,
s János úgy eltikkadt a szomjúságtól, hogy a nyelvét is kivetette.
Gondolja magában: itt a tehén, megfeji s vége a szomjúságnak.
Megköti a tehenet egy fához s merthogy sajtár nem volt vele (már honnét is lett volna),
vette a sapkáját, a tehén tőgye alá tartotta s elkezdette fejni.
Fejte, fejte, de biz' egy csepp nem sok, annyi tej sem cseppent.

An argument or bullying?

Bullying is when someone hurts another person again and again, on purpose, and the other one cannot easily defend themselves. It can be words, leaving someone out, rumours, or online. A one-off argument is not bullying, but if it hurt, you can talk about that too.
Prickly, don't sit here! This seat is taken!
Nobody wants to sit with me...
How might Hedgy feel now? (You can pick more than one.)
Lonely, because she sits alone.
Yes. If she is always left alone, she gets lonelier and lonelier.
Sad, because the words hurt.
Yes. Words can hurt too, even when you cannot see it.
Scared it will happen again tomorrow.
Yes. When it happens again and again, you start to fear it will never stop.
Fine, it is only a joke.
Are you sure? Look how she curls up. If only one side is laughing, it is not a joke. How else might she feel?
2. The audience
In the dining hall Magpie teases Hedgy again: "Look, Prickly eats alone again!" Some laugh. With every laugh Magpie gets louder. What do you do when you see this?
You did not laugh. Froggy did not either. Magpie looked around, but nobody laughed with her. She went quiet. Hedgy looked up and smiled at you for a moment.
Laughing counts too
Whoever laughs, or just watches, is part of the audience. Bullying grows from the audience. If we do not laugh along, the audience is gone, and the one being hurt sees that they are not alone.
Look, she eats alone again! Haha!
You are not laughing?
Some are laughing in the dining hall. What do you do? (You can pick more than one.)
I keep a straight face and don't laugh along.
Magpie looked at you, but got no laugh from you. The audience is one smaller.
I go and sit next to Hedgy for lunch.
Hedgy moved her tray to make room. Now there are two of you.
I tell the teacher on lunch duty.
The teacher came over, and Magpie stopped. That is not telling tales, it is asking for help.
I laugh too, everybody does.
It is so easy to laugh along. But Hedgy hears every laugh, and they make Magpie louder. What would you rather do?
3. Four ways

At break Magpie spread a rumour that Hedgy popped the ball with her spines. It is not true. "Hedgy can't play with us!" says Magpie. Hedgy sits alone on the bench. Type, then decide what you would do!
Whichever way you choose, Hedgy is not alone any more. And you do not have to sort it all out alone: the adults help too.
Four ways to stand up

1. Say something, if it is safe: "That's not okay." 2. Distract: invite the one being hurt to play. 3. Get help from an adult: that is not telling tales. 4. Be there afterwards: ask if they are okay. Your own safety comes first. If one adult does not help, tell another one.
Hedgy popped the ball! She can't play with us!
But it wasn't me...
If something is wrong, you can always tell me.
Hedgy sits alone on the bench. What do you do? (You can pick more than one.)
I say: "That's not true, and Hedgy can play."
You said it calmly. Froggy stood next to you, and Magpie had nothing to say. This is good when you feel safe.
I ask Hedgy to come and draw with me.
Hedgy's eyes lit up. You drew a huge dragon in chalk, and slowly others came to look.
I ask Mrs Owl, our teacher, for help.
Mrs Owl thanked you for telling her. That is not telling tales: it is asking for help so someone is safe.
Later I ask Hedgy if she is okay.
Hedgy said it hurt, and that she was glad you asked. One question can mean a lot.
I do nothing.
That is understandable, sometimes we are scared too. But silence helps Magpie, not Hedgy. Which small step could you try?
4. The class chat
In the evening a picture of Hedgy appeared in the class chat, with a mean caption. Magpie sent it. Three have already put a laughing face on it. Hedgy is in the group too, and she can see it.
The next day the picture was gone from the group. Hedgy came to school and saw that several classmates were on her side.
Online counts too
Online the same rule counts. Do not send it on, and do not laugh at it. Take a screenshot, block, report, and show it to an adult. Write something kind to the classmate who was hurt.
It's just a joke! Send it on!
Everybody saw the picture...
The mean picture is in the group. What do you do? (You can pick more than one.)
I don't send it on, and I don't laugh at it.
The picture stopped with you. If nobody sends it on, it goes no further.
I take a screenshot and show it to Mum.
Mum took it seriously. She showed the class teacher, and the picture was gone that same evening.
I write something kind to Hedgy.
"I think your drawing is great" you wrote. Hedgy answered with a smiling hedgehog.
I put a laughing face on it too.
One laughing face seems small, but it hurts Hedgy and cheers Magpie on. Online we are part of the audience too. What would you rather do?
5. Making it right
The next day Mrs Owl sat down to talk with the class. She did not shout, and she did not call anyone bad. She asked: what happened, and how did everyone feel? Magpie was quiet for a long time.

At last Magpie spoke: "I wanted everyone to notice me. I didn't think Hedgy felt so bad." She said sorry, and helped Hedgy put her drawings up in the corridor. Together the class wrote a rule on the wall: Here everyone is fine just as they are.
You are fine as you are
Hurtful behaviour can change. It is not the child who is bad but what they did, so saying sorry and putting things right are part of the answer. Together a class decides: here, that is not okay.
What happened, and how did everyone feel?
I didn't think it hurt her so much...
Shall we put my drawings up together?
What can Magpie do to make it right? (You can pick more than one.)
Say sorry, and mean it.
A real sorry says what happened, and that you regret it.
Help Hedgy put her drawings up.
Actions count too: Hedgy sees that Magpie really wants to change.
Be kind next time, and keep watching out.
Change shows in the days after. We can help her with that too.
Nothing, it does not matter now.
It matters to Hedgy. Making it right means Magpie does something too. What could she do?
Hedgy does not curl up any more. Magpie has new friends, and now she is the first to say when something is not okay. Thank you for standing up!

The Star Coins
Once upon a time there was a little girl.
This little girl had no father
and no mother, and she was left as poor in this world as a church mouse.
She did not even have a little house to live in, nor a little bed
to lie down in; she had nothing but her clothes,
just the ones she wore, and a single piece of bread:
even that was given to her by a kind-hearted man.
With nothing else to do, the little girl set off, hoping the good Lord would help her.
As she walked and walked across the meadow, a poor man came up to her and begged:
"Good little girl, give me something to eat. I have not had a bite for three days."
The little girl did not think twice; she gave her bread to the poor man.
"God bless you," said the poor man gratefully, and went on his way.
The girl went on too, and a child came up to her, crying bitterly, and begged:
"Give me something to cover my head with, my head is so cold!"
Without a word, the little girl gave the child her hat.
She walked on and on, and again a child came up to her
who had not a single piece of clothing on.
She did not wait to be asked; she gave the child her little coat.
Then she came into the forest.
Evening was just falling, and a child came up to her and asked
for her little shirt, or else the cold would surely be the end of him.
The little girl said to herself:
"It is dark anyway, no one can see. You can give away your shirt."
And so she gave it.
Now she truly had nothing at all.
There she stood, standing still, and looked up at the starry sky,
she sighed a deep sigh, and listen to this wonder! one by one the stars fell,
thick as rain, and when they touched the ground they all became pure white silver coins.
And from the sky there fell a lovely linen shirt too,
so white and so fine that it was a wonder to see.
She gathered up the coins, and from then on she had no more worries: she lived happily.
Tomorrow the little girl shall be your guest.

Peterke
Once there was a poor man.
This poor man had as many children as a sieve has holes, and one more.
The poor fellow did not even know whom to ask to be godfather to his newborn son,
because even the priest and the cantor were already godfathers to his children.
Oh, what a poor world, what a hard bed!
So the poor man set off with many sighs to look for a godfather.
By evening he reached a great forest, and he got so lost in it
that he could not find his way out at all.
He wandered this way and that, and all at once he met a tiny little man,
whose beard was two yards long and dragged along the ground behind him.
The poor man was frightened,
for he had never in all his life seen such a strange creature.
The tiny man spoke to him:
"What are you doing here, friend?
What is your business?"
The poor man was even more frightened.
"Well, this must be the devil," he thought to himself,
"and he will take me down, God knows where!"
He answered him:
"Oh, my dear tiny little man, my life and death are in your hands.
I set out to look for a godfather, because I have as many children
as a sieve has holes, and one more; the priest is already a godfather to them,
and the cantor too; not a single soul will agree to be a godfather."
The tiny man said:
"Do not fret over that! I will be that child's godfather!
I ask only one thing: when he is seven years, seven months,
seven weeks and seven days old, give the boy to me, and I will take good care of him."
The poor man agreed.
He thought God had given him plenty of children; one given away would hardly be missed.
With that they turned around and went to the poor man's house,
and the child was baptised Peter.
His godfather at once bought him such baby clothes
that not even the king's child had finer ones.
Well, time went by.
All at once Peterke's parents noticed
that the time was nearly up when they had to give their child to the tiny man.
Oh! The poor man shed many bitter tears,
but his wife shed even more; they grieved and sighed a great deal
over why they had to part with this dear child of their hearts,
for there was no child so handsome, with black hair and black eyes, so clever-handed,
so wise as he was.
But all their grieving was in vain, in vain they shed so many bitter tears,
Peterke became seven years, seven months,
seven weeks and seven days old, and he had to be taken to his godfather.
The poor man said to his wife:
"Well, wife, bake me a cake in the ashes. The time has come,
what I promised seven years ago, I cannot take back!"
The poor woman cried, she cried bitterly, but she baked the cake all the same,
got her husband ready for the road, and he took Peterke away.
They walked and walked, and by evening they reached the great forest.
When they were deep inside, the earth opened before them, and out popped the tiny man.
He did not even let the poor man speak; he snatched Peterke from him,
and through the opening he had come out of, he vanished with him.
And the poor man set off home in great sorrow.
For fourteen whole days the tiny man carried his godson downwards,
and on the fourteenth day they reached a meadow
where golden grass grew, diamond flowers bloomed and golden horses grazed.
But, so I don't mix up my words, by then Peterke had grown into a fine, big lad.
For three days they went on through this land, across golden meadows everywhere,
through golden forests and past golden fish ponds.
On the third day they came to a castle that turned on a diamond leg.
Here the tiny man struck the castle gate with a golden rod,
the gate opened at once, and he himself turned a somersault over his head,
and lo, he became a young lady so wonderfully beautiful
that you could look at the sun, but not at her.
Peter could not say a word; he was so amazed he could not speak.
Then the beautiful young lady said:
"Listen, handsome lad!
A wicked old witch put a curse on me that I should be a tiny man
until I found a bridegroom seven years, seven months, seven weeks and seven days old.
Now I have found you, and if you will have me, look, do you see this fine kingdom?
It will all be yours!"
And Peterke had not a single word against that.
At once they harnessed six diamond-haired horses to a diamond coach,
drove up in a moment to Peter's family, brought down his father,
his mother and all his brothers and sisters to the land of happiness,
there they held a great feast, and they are still alive today, if they have not died.
Doctor Know-All
There was once a poor man, and his name was Crab.
One day this poor man took a cartload of wood into town and sold it to a doctor.
The doctor was just sitting at the table
when he paid for the wood, and the poor man nearly ate the fine food with his eyes
and the drink that was on the table.
He thought to himself: oh, how well off doctors are!
If only I could be a doctor, then I would live like a gentleman too,
I would eat and drink all day, and no one would be happier than me!
Whatever he thought, he went and asked the doctor:
"Tell me, could I not become a doctor too?"
"Of course you could," answered the doctor.
"Nothing is easier.
First of all, buy an ABC book, that one,
you know, the one with a rooster painted at the front;
sell your ox and your cart, and with the money buy doctor's clothes and everything
that a doctor needs.
Above all, do not forget to buy spectacles.
Then you will look like a real doctor.
Then have a big sign made, and have this written on it:
Here lives the Know-All Doctor. And nail this sign to your gate."
The peasant went home and did everything, to the last letter, as the doctor advised.
And soon the fame of the Know-All Doctor spread across seven times seven lands,
and even a lame step beyond that.
Word went everywhere that Master Crab knew everything,
that there was no secret in the world he could not find out.
No, there was none.
Once it happened that a great lord's money was stolen.
When it could not be found anywhere, someone told the great lord
that in such-and-such a place there was a know-all doctor,
called Crab; he should send for him, and he would tell where the money was.
Well, the great lord did not need telling twice; he had his horses harnessed,
drove to the know-all doctor, went in and asked if what they said about him was true.
"Every word of it is true," said Master Crab.
They agreed at once, and Master Crab was taken to the lord's castle, and his wife too,
and there they were seated at once in the finest room,
the table was laid, and Master Crab and his wife sat down at it.
As they sat down, the first servant brought in a dish, and Master Crab nudged his wife.
"Here is the first."
The servant nearly dropped the dish, he was so frightened.
He thought the know-all doctor meant: here is the first thief.
And indeed he was a thief, and so were the other servants.
The servant went out and said to the others: "We are done for!
The doctor knows everything.
As I came in, he said to his wife: that is the first!"
The second servant did not want to go in at all, but he had to go in all the same.
As he came in with the dish, Master Crab nudged his wife:
"This is the second!"
It was a wonder of God that the servant did not drop the dish, he was so frightened.
"We are done for," he said outside, "this man really does know everything.
When I came in, he said: this is the second."
The third one fared just the same.
The fourth servant had to carry in a covered dish; the lord went in too,
because he wanted to test whether the doctor knew what was in the dish.
Oh, how the poor doctor sweated,
he scratched his head, and in his misery he sighed: oh, poor Crab!
"That's right," said the lord with great joy, "there really is crab in it.
Now I believe that you know where the money is, too."
The lord went out, and the servants came at once, called out the doctor, surrounded him,
and confessed that the four of them had stolen the money;
they would give him a share, if only he did not give them away.
They even showed him where they had hidden the money.
With that Master Crab went back into his room.
The lord was there again and asked: well, what news, doctor?
Master Crab sat down at the table, took out his ABC book,
pushed his spectacles up on his forehead and said:
"I will look it up in this book at once."
Meanwhile, so I don't forget, the fifth servant had hidden in the stove,
for he wanted to hear whether the doctor really knew everything.
Master Crab began to turn the pages back and forth, looking for the rooster picture.
For a long time he could not find the rooster, and he angrily struck the book.
"I know you are in here, you must come out."
The fifth servant thought he was talking about him,
he jumped out of the stove in terrible fright and cried: He really does know everything!
Then Master Crab shut the book and led the lord to the place
where the servants had hidden the money,
and the lord paid him well, and the servants paid him well too,
he could hardly carry it all, he got so much money.
So it was, it is over, it was a tale.
Whoever does not believe it can go and see for himself.
Which Is Worth More?
Over there, down a little, up a little, beyond the Tisza, beyond the Danube,
where the short-tailed spotted pig digs, there once was a king who had three sons.
When all three sons had grown up so much
that their moustaches began to sprout, the king said to them:
- Now, my dear sons, it is time for you to go and see the wide world!
The three princes set off on three fine horses, over hills and valleys,
through forests and fields, now downhill, now uphill, but always onward.
They went on and on, until one day they came to a huge city.
At the edge of the city they asked a boy:
- Hey, boy, what sort of town is this village?
The boy answered that this was the city of the White King.
The princes were glad to reach a king's city, and went straight to the palace,
and there before the king, and told him who they were and where they came from.
The White King was glad to see them, for he was good friends with their father.
But the princes were even gladder when they saw the White King's daughter.
They had seen many lovely girls at home, but none as lovely as this.
All three crowded around her and showed off, and when supper was over,
all three went into the king's room, and all three asked for his daughter's hand.
"Now which one should I give her to?
the king wondered.
Oh, oh, if only I had two more daughters!"
What could he do?
He did not want to make any of them angry, so he said:
- Listen, lads, I will not give my daughter to any of you now. Go on your way,
and whoever comes back a year from today with the most useful thing will have her.
Here is my hand on it, and my word is good.
The lads shook hands on it, and set off at dawn.
They rode together until they came to a great wild forest.
There the road split three ways, so they agreed to go three different ways,
and to meet again at this very spot in a year's time.
They parted in peace, and each went his own way.
All three lads travelled through many lands, and looked at everything closely,
they bought this and that, then threw it away when they found something better.
But time went by, and they had to turn back,
and in the end each of the three settled on one thing,
and by the time the year was up,
they were back in the great forest where they had parted.
Of course they wanted to see at once what each had brought.
The eldest said:
- Look, I bought a spyglass that lets you see to the end of the world.
The middle one said:
- I bought a cloak that you only have to wrap yourself in,
and it flies you in the blink of an eye wherever you tell it.
The third one said:
- And I bought an orange, and if a dead person,
not yet dead for twenty-four hours,
has it held under their nose, they wake up at once.
As they told each other this, the eldest looked into his spyglass,
and, dear Lord, he dropped it from his hand in fright.
- Did you see something bad?
asked his brothers.
- Oh, don't even ask, the princess is lying dead!
The other two looked into the spyglass too,
and it was true: the lovely princess was lying dead.
- Quick, quick, cried the middle prince, get under my cloak,
we will be there at once, and maybe she can still be brought back to life!
They got under the cloak, and hop! they were already in the king's palace.
The youngest prince took out the orange and held it under the princess's nose,
and look, at once her eyes flew open and her lips smiled!
Oh, how happy everyone was.
They were, but not for long.
For the princes began to quarrel over the girl.
The eldest said:
- She belongs to me, for I saw that she was dead.
The middle one said:
- You could have seen it all you liked:
without my cloak we would still be in the forest.
The girl belongs to me.
- Is that so?
said the youngest.
- And what good would it have been that one of us saw her
and the other flew us here, without my orange?
The king could not judge between them, so he had
to call together the wise men of the land, to let them judge.
They sat down together and talked for seven days and seven nights,
one said this, the other said that,
until on the seventh night they agreed after all
that the princess belonged to the youngest prince.
The older brothers accepted this too,
and danced at their brother's wedding so hard that the palace floor shook.
Then, in the middle of all the fun, the eldest took out his spyglass
and peeked into it.
- Come here, come, he said to his brother with the cloak, look in, what do you see?
- I see, said he, two lovely girls, like two shining stars.
- Well, if you see them, let's get under the cloak and take a closer look!
They had hardly thought of it when they were already there.
And yes, those two girls were king's daughters too.
They asked for their hands, got them, and carried them off in the cloak.
They did not stop until they were home.
By then their younger brother had come home too, with his wife.
Now there was a truly merry wedding.
Even the lame kicked up the dust as best they could.
There were plates and bowls enough, little food and drink, yet all was well.
Salt
Once upon a time there was an old king who had three lovely daughters.
The king already had one foot in the grave,
and he wished to see all three of his daughters married.
That would not have been hard, for he had three kingdoms,
so each of his daughters would get one kingdom.
But just as no three apples are the same, the three kingdoms were not the same either.
So one day the king said to his daughters
that he would give the finest kingdom to the one who loved him best.
He asked the girls one by one, starting with the eldest:
- Tell me, my dear daughter, how much do you love me?
- As the dove loves clean wheat, said the girl.
- And you, my dear daughter?
he asked the middle one.
- I love you, dear father, as one loves a breeze in the hot summer.
- Now I ask you, he turned to the youngest, tell me, how do you love me?
- As people love salt, dear father!
answered the little princess.
- What are you saying, you worthless child! snapped the king,
get out of my court, and out of my kingdom too!
I never want to see you again, if that is all you love me!
In vain the princess wept and begged, in vain she explained
how much people love salt, in every way -
there was no mercy and no pardon: the little princess had to go out into the world.
The little princess set off, weeping bitterly, and wandered into a great forest.
She could not find her way out, so she made her home in a hollow tree,
and picked strawberries, raspberries, blackberries, hazelnuts, and lived there alone.
One day, when a whole year had passed, the prince of the next kingdom came by,
and he caught sight of the princess among the raspberry bushes.
But the princess saw the prince too, and in great fright ran into the hollow tree.
The prince went after her and called in:
- Who is in here?
The princess hid in the hollow, trembling
like an aspen leaf, and she did not say a single word.
The prince asked again:
- Hey!
Who is in here?
Are you a person or a devil?
If a person, come out; if a devil, go down to the bottom of hell!
The princess still did not dare to speak.
The prince asked a third time:
- Hey!
Who is in here?
Speak!
Are you a person or a devil? For I will shoot in at once!
At this the princess was terribly frightened,
and she crept out of the hollow tree, sniffling and sobbing.
Her dress was ragged and dirty, and she was very ashamed,
and with bitter tears she told the prince who she was.
The prince liked the princess very much, for however ragged she was,
however dirty her dress, her face was lovely and sweet.
He took her hand very gently and led her home to his palace,
and there he dressed her in a rich gold dress
set with diamonds, and he did not wait two weeks, not even one, I think,
not even a day, maybe not even an hour: he sent for a priest, they were married,
and they held such a great wedding that, well ... who could say how great it was.
Time went by, and the young couple lived together in peace,
and loved each other like two doves.
One day the king said:
- Now, wife, when I first saw you,
I did not really ask why your father had sent you away.
Tell me the plain truth!
- My dear husband, said the queen,
I can only tell you now what I told him then.
My father asked how I loved him, and I said: as people love salt.
- Very well, said the king, I will do something,
and I know your father's heart will turn back to you.
How he would turn it back, he did not tell his wife,
but he went into the other room,
wrote a letter to the old king, and asked him to come to lunch.
The letter went the next day, and on the third day the old king came in a coach and six.
The young king led the old king up into the palace,
into the finest room of the palace, where the table was already laid for two.
They sat down at the table, and the servants brought one fine dish after another,
but so that I do not mix up my words,
the young king had given orders
that every dish for the old king be cooked separately,
and baked, and that no salt be put in it.
Well, that was some lunch!
The old king tasted the soup, took one spoonful, then two,
but put the spoon down at once: he could not eat the soup, it had no salt at all.
The old king thought to himself: they must have forgotten the salt in this,
but there will surely be some in the boiled beef.
There was not even a poppy seed's worth in that.
They brought in the roasts one after another, but they could take them back again,
for the old king only gave each a little lick
and did not bite into it, so bland and salt-free was every costly roast.
This the old king could not bear without a word.
- Listen, my young friend, what kind of cook do you have, who cooks without salt?
- He always cooks with salt at other times, Your Majesty,
but I heard that Your Majesty does not love salt,
so I ordered that his head would be cut off if he put even a poppy seed of salt in.
- Well, my young friend, you did wrong there, for I love salt very much.
Who told you that I do not love it?
- Why, your very own daughter, Your Majesty, said the young king.
At that very moment the door opened,
and in came the queen, the old king's youngest daughter.
Oh, dear God, how glad the old king was!
For long ago he had come to regret, with all his heart, sending his daughter away,
and since then he had had her searched for all over the world.
And so, of course, he now gave his youngest daughter his biggest kingdom.
The young king took this kingdom into his care as well,
and they are still alive today, if they have not died.
The Seven Ravens
Once there was a man who had seven sons.
This man always prayed that God would bless him with a little daughter too.
God heard his many prayers, and gave him a lovely little baby girl.
But the little girl was so weak when she was born
that they feared she would not live even one day.
Quickly they sent the seven sons to fetch fresh spring water from the forest,
to christen the child with it, so that she would not die unchristened.
The boys ran into the forest, but when they reached the spring,
each wanted to be the first to fill the jug, and the jug fell into the well.
In it went, and because the well was deep, they could not get the jug out.
The poor boys were sad, not knowing what to do now.
They did not dare go home, so they stayed in the forest,
and their father could not imagine what had happened to them.
- They must have started playing, he said, and forgotten all about the water.
Still the boys did not come, and their father grew angrier and angrier.
In his great anger,
that now the little girl would die unchristened, he began to curse:
- I wish all seven of them would turn into ravens!
The words had hardly left his mouth when he heard loud chattering and cawing.
The man looked up, and there were seven black ravens flying above him.
Oh, dear God, a great heavy sorrow fell upon the man's heart,
and an even greater one upon his wife's heart.
They wept and wailed and tore their hair, but no matter: their sons stayed ravens.
Still, they were lucky that the little girl did not die,
but grew stronger and prettier from day to day.
For a long time the little girl did not know that she had brothers,
but one day she happened to hear from the neighbours
that she had had seven brothers and they had become ravens because of her.
Oh, dear God, how sad this made the little girl!
She ran to her father and mother and asked:
- Is it true, my dear parents, that I had seven brothers?
Where are they, what became of them?
- Well, there is no denying it, said her father, you had seven brothers,
but the poor boys were turned into ravens when you were born.
We will weep for them until we die.
From that moment on the little girl had no peace.
She felt her brothers became ravens because of her, and she made a vow -
come what may -
that she would not rest
until she had found her brothers and freed them from the curse.
She told her parents what she meant to do,
but oh, how they wept and wailed then!
Was it not enough that they had lost seven dear, handsome sons,
must they now lose their only daughter too?
But all their weeping was in vain, the little girl could not stay at home.
She had a little ring her parents had given her to remember them, she took only that,
and a piece of bread and a jug of water: and so she set out into the world.
On and on went the little girl, over hills and valleys, through forest
and across fields, on and on she went, until she came to the very end of the world.
But there at the end of the world the sun shone so hot
that the little girl ran on in terror: she thought she would burn to ashes on the spot.
She ran to the moon, but it was so cold that she nearly froze.
The poor thing ran on in a panic and did not stop until she reached the stars.
They twinkled and smiled so kindly, sat her down among them, and asked what she wanted,
how she had come here, and when she told them
that she was looking for her brothers, the Evening Star said:
- Well, you have come to the right place, little girl.
Your seven brothers are on the Ice Mountain.
Here, I will give you a little key,
with it you will open the Ice Mountain gate, and there you will find your brothers.
She thanked them nicely for the gift,
said goodbye to the stars, and ran up the Ice Mountain like the swift wind.
At the top she looked and looked for the key to open the door, but could not find it.
Oh, dear God, what could she do now?
How could she free her brothers?
She thought and thought, then took her little knife and cut off her little finger,
put it into the gate, and look, at that very moment it opened.
She went through the gate, but after two steps a dwarf stood before her and asked:
- What are you looking for here, little girl?
The little girl answered:
- I am looking for my brothers, the seven ravens, dear dwarf.
Are they here?
- Here, yes, said the dwarf, but they are not at home just now.
But if you want to wait for them until they come home, then come in.
They went into the seven ravens' room, and there the dwarf laid the table,
set out seven plates, seven cups, food on all seven plates, drink in all seven cups.
The little girl tasted the food of all seven, one by one,
she ate a little from each of the seven plates,
she drank from the cups too, and into the last cup she dropped her ring.
All at once the little girl heard a great flapping of wings
and cawing, and the dwarf announced:
- Now, little girl, here come the raven lords!
And in came the ravens, flying through the door,
they sat down at the table and began to eat,
but they saw at once that someone had eaten their food and drunk their drink.
- Who has eaten and who has drunk here? they asked each other.
It was a person, that is certain.
Then the youngest raven happened to look at the bottom of his cup, and saw the ring.
- Look, a ring! he cried.
This was our parents' ring!
Look!
- So it is!
This is our parents' ring! they all cried in great wonder.
- Oh, dear God, said the eldest,
if only our little sister were here, we would be freed from the curse at once!
At that very moment the little girl ran out from behind the door, where she had hidden,
and, hear this wonder, the seven ravens turned into boys at once!
And what handsome boys they were!
One by one they hugged and kissed the little girl, then without
a word more they set off home, and did not stop until they got there.
And then at home!
That was where the real joy was!
They are all still alive today, if they have not died.
The King of the Birds
Tale, tale, I tell a tale now about the birds, and the birds' terrible great battle...
It happened like this:
once the bear and the wolf were walking in the forest, and as they wandered about,
they heard a lovely, lovely bird song.
The bear stopped in wonder, opened his eyes and mouth wide, and listened to the song.
Then he asked the wolf:
"Tell me, friend wolf, what bird is it that sings so beautifully?"
"That is the king of the birds," said the wolf.
"Later we will go to him and pay our respects."
"Good," agreed the bear, "I have never seen a royal palace anyway. Let's go."
"Oho, it is not as easy as that," said the wolf,
"we must wait until the queen comes home."
A minute passed, then two, and the queen came,
carrying food in her beak; the king came too,
and his beak was full as well, and then they flew into a hollow in a tree:
that was the palace, I mean to say, the nest.
The bear wanted to climb up at once, but the wolf pulled him back:
"Oho, stop.
Wait until they have both gone away."
Very well, the bear agreed, and they walked on,
but first they took a good look at the hollow of the tree where the nest was.
But the bear could not rest, and after a little while they went back to the tree.
By then the king and the queen had indeed flown out of the nest,
so the bear climbed up the tree, looked into the hole and saw
that there were five baby birds in the nest.
"Is this a royal palace?"
grumbled the bear.
"Well, what a shabby palace it is! And are these royal children?
Why, they are just common peasant brats!"
Oh, the little birds flew into a terrible rage at these insulting words.
Beside themselves, they shouted and chirped:
"We are not peasant brats,
we are true royal children, you should know that, you grumbling bear!
Just you wait, you will be sorry for these words!"
The bear was startled at this, and so was the wolf,
and they slunk back to their cave, deeply worried about what would happen now.
Meanwhile the king of the birds came home, and the queen too,
but they were nearly scared to death when they heard the children's terrible chirping.
The eldest spoke, and then the others after him:
"The bear was here and he said
that we are not royal children, but common peasant brats.
Until we know what the real truth is, we will not move our beaks
or our wings, and we will starve to death right here in this place,
but we will not live in shame."
"Now, now," said the king, shaking his head, "what sort of talk is this?
My father was a king, and my grandfather, back to the seventy-seventh one.
Just calm down, and I will show that old peasant who and what I am."
He did not stay at home for even a blink of an eye,
he flew with his followers to the bear's cave and called in:
"Listen, you old honey thief, how dare you insult my children?
Know that I declare war on you, and woe to you and all your kin!"
Now this was no joke at all.
Friend bear got up and sent word to the four-legged animals to get on their feet,
because the king of the birds had declared war, and it would be such a war
as there had never been since the world began.
And it was good that they got on their feet,
because within an hour the king of the birds gathered every bird in the world,
and not only the birds, but even the beetles, the bees and the flies,
every kind of creature that had wings.
When the army had gathered, the king of the birds sent out the wren
to spy and find out who would be the leader of the enemy.
Away flew the wren,
hid under a leaf on a tree beside the bear's cave, and listened.
Along came the bear, very grumpy, growling and grumbling, called the fox and said:
"Listen, fox, you are the cleverest of all the animals,
you must lead the army."
"Good," said the fox, "but what shall the signal be?"
One said one thing, another said another,
at last the fox suggested something that everyone liked.
He said:
"I have a fine, long, bushy tail, it will do well as a flag.
If I hold my tail up high, it means: follow me!
If my tail droops down, then: run away wherever you can."
The wren flew back at once and reported what he had heard.
"Very well, come on then, friend fox," said the bird king, "your tail will droop!"
Early the next morning the battle began.
The four-legged animals set off with a terrible roar,
(the donkey was among them) with a dreadful braying,
(the ox was among them too), and heaven and earth rang and shook with it.
But the birds set off too, the air whirred and buzzed with the beating of their wings,
the forest rang and echoed, oh, what will happen here, Lord Jesus Christ!
Then the king of the birds at once sent out a few stag beetles,
and they flew straight at the fox,
one here, the other there, pinching and stabbing him with their horns,
the fox goes this way and that, holding his tail up high,
but only with pain and trouble, and the others rush after him,
then all at once the fox's tail droops down,
and off they go, run for your lives, the four-legged army fled head over heels,
as if they had all gone blind!
The king and the queen flew home at once and said with great joy:
"Now, children, don't be sad, eat and drink, we have won the battle!"
The children said:
"Not until the bear comes here and says sorry to us."
"The children are right,"
said the king, and he flew at once to the bear's cave and called in:
"Listen, you old honey thief, come before my nest and ask my children to forgive you,
or else I will put you to a terrible death."
Whether the bear liked it or not,
he slunk to the nest and, weeping, begged the royal children to forgive him.
And now the children ate and drank and were merry,
the forest rang with it, they sang like that all day long.
That's how it was!
The Miller's Boy and the Cat
It was not here, it was not there, but somewhere it was:
there was once a mill, and in it a miller,
who had no wife and no children,
only two miller lads and a little apprentice boy with him.
One day the miller said to the lads:
"Listen, lads, I have grown old, my place is now beside the fire.
Go out, and whichever of you brings me the best horse,
to him I will give the mill, and all I ask is that he look after me until I die."
The lads jumped at this offer, and they set off that very day,
not only the big lads, but even the little apprentice, though they mocked him a lot:
"And you, what do you want?
Sit by the stove, stay at home,
you will never get a horse, not while the world lasts and two days more."
But let them talk and mock, the little apprentice, whose name was Jancsi,
went with them, stumbling after them over hill and valley.
By evening they reached a cave, went in and lay down, but the two lads only waited
for Jancsi to fall asleep, then they crept out of the cave and left Jancsi there.
In the morning Jancsi woke up, looked around, and saw no one,
and he grew very sad: what should he do now?
Well, he got up and felt his way out of the cave,
and set off all alone: come what may, perhaps God will be with him.
As he walked along on his own, a little spotted cat came towards him and spoke:
"Where are you going, little Jancsi?"
"Don't even ask," said Jancsi, "you can't help me anyway."
"Can't I?
You see, I know what you wish for.
You want to get a fine horse.
Come with me, enter my service, and if you serve me faithfully for seven years,
I will give you a horse so fine that it has no match across seven plains."
"Hm," thought Jancsi, "this must be some magic cat, maybe it is telling the truth."
He did not think long, he took service with the cat and went to her little palace.
Oh, and how many cats there were, dear good God!
Hundreds of them jumped and frolicked up and down the stairs,
inside in the rooms, outside in the yard, everywhere.
There were so many that Jancsi's eyes could not take them all in.
And even more in the evening, when they sat down to the table.
They played music so that the palace rang with it, and when supper was over,
the little spotted cat sprang in front of Jancsi and called:
"Come, Jancsi, dance with me."
"No, I do not dance with a cat," said Jancsi, "I have never done that in my life!"
"Then put him to bed," the little spotted cat ordered the others.
They gathered round him, led him to his room, pulled off his boots, put him to bed.
In the morning they came in again, dressed him and washed him,
and wiped his face with their little tails.
In a word, Jancsi had a good life.
He thought that since he had taken service, he ought to do some work too.
The little spotted cat gave him a silver axe,
a golden scythe and a diamond rake.
With the axe he chopped wood, with the scythe he cut grass for the horses (oh,
what horses there were in the stable!),
with the rake he raked up the hay, well,
no one could complain: if they kept him well, he worked for it too.
When the seven years were over, the little spotted cat called Jancsi into the stable:
there stood seven steeds in a row, all with golden coats, and she said to him:
"Now, Jancsi, of the seven horses choose the one
that pleases your eyes and your heart the most.
Then go home, and in three days I will bring your horse after you."
Jancsi chose the most beautiful steed,
said goodbye to the little spotted cat and walked home nicely on foot.
He went home just as he had come, in the same clothes,
because the little spotted cat gave him nothing else:
she said he should just go home ragged and dirty, that would be best.
And ragged he was indeed!
In seven years his clothes had worn away so much
that only rags and tatters hung from his body.
And of course the lads were already at home: one had got a blind old nag,
the other a lame one, but no matter, they had got something after all.
Oh, how they laughed at Jancsi!
"Didn't we tell you to stay at home?"
Jancsi went into the mill and greeted the miller,
but the miller barely greeted him back, did not even let him sit down,
he chased him out of the house and said: there is the goose shed, let him live in that,
he would not sit at one table with such a ragged, dirty lad.
"Fine," thought Jancsi, "this will change yet," and he went to the shed without a word,
lay down there and slept like a log till morning.
That very morning it was three days
since he had left his service, and as the sun rose,
there came a golden coach with six horses, and beside it a groom with the seventh horse.
The coach stopped, and look, out stepped a beautiful, beautiful princess;
it was the little spotted cat, whom Jancsi had served for seven years.
She asked the miller:
"Where is the little miller's boy?"
The miller answered:
"Out in the goose shed.
We don't let him into the house, he is so dirty, so ragged."
"Then call him here," ordered the princess.
Meanwhile, from the coach they took out beautiful golden
clothes with diamonds, they washed Jancsi,
combed his hair with a golden comb, then dressed him in the golden
clothes with diamonds: not even a prince could look finer than Jancsi.
Then the princess wanted to see
what kind of horses the miller lads had brought.
Well, one was lame, the other blind.
"Bring the seventh steed here," she ordered the servants.
"Well, I have never seen such a fine horse in all my life!" cried the miller.
"If you haven't, then know that it belongs to the little miller's boy."
"Then the mill is his too," said the miller.
"My palace is his, not your mill," said the princess.
And with that she and Jancsi got into the coach and drove off to the little palace.
Little palace, did I say?
It had grown into a palace so big that it had seventy-seven windows,
of pure silver, its door was gold, its stairs were diamond.
There they held a great wedding at once, and danced for seven days and seven nights.
Tomorrow may they be your guests.
Ashy Jutka
Once upon a time there was a poor widow.
This woman had only one daughter, but she did not have much joy even in her.
This girl was so lazy that word of it spread beyond seven counties.
From morning till evening she sat in the ashes, poking at them,
stirring them with her fingers, and the village folk named her Ashy Jutka.
Oh dear, oh dear, how the poor widow fretted!
Being a widow was not enough, her daughter had to be lazy too.
All her kind words were in vain: you should work too, my daughter,
at something; at least spin one spindle of hemp a day!
She could talk all she liked: in one ear and out the other.
Then one day the poor woman ran out of patience,
she grabbed her distaff, with both hands, and gave Jutka a sound beating.
"There, take that!
Do you want more?"
Oh, how Jutka cried, the whole village rang with her crying, and she told her mother
that she would not beat her any more, because she was going out into the world.
"Go with God, and have a good road with no mud!"
Jutka did go, but as she stepped out into the street crying loudly,
who should come along but the prince in a coach with six horses.
He stopped the coach and asked the poor woman:
"Tell me, good mother, why did you beat your daughter?"
The widow answered:
"Because, if you please, I cannot get enough hemp for her,
she has already spun even the thatch of my garden shed, and she still wants to spin.
Too much of a good thing is too much!"
"Really, is this girl truly such a good spinner?"
said the prince, "then let her come to me, there is spinning for her there.
A great granary is full of hemp, and if she spins it all in one month,
here is my hand on it, I will make her my wife."
"Well now," thought the woman, "nothing will come of that,
but take her away!" The girl thought just the same,
but she got into the coach all the same, in case some wonder of the world might happen.
When they arrived at the king's palace,
the prince at once took Jutka into the granary.
He said:
"Now, Jutka, here you can spin as much as you like.
What I said, I said: if you spin in one month
all the hemp that is here, I will make you my wife."
Jutka could not even speak, she was so scared at the sight of that sea of hemp.
Why, she could not spin this in a thousand years.
She cried and grieved day and night.
One day passed after another, one week went by, then two,
then three, but not a single thread of the hemp was missing.
The little serving boy who brought her food asked when she would start spinning,
but Jutka only answered: there is still plenty of time for that.
But when she was alone in the granary, she cried like a rain shower.
How could she have been such a great fool as to sit down in the granary!
Soon the month would be over,
and the prince might even have her head cut off in his anger, for making a fool of him.
Just as she was thinking about this, all of a sudden,
good God knows from where, a teeny-tiny dwarf popped up in front of her.
But this dwarf had a beard seven yards long,
and wherever he went, he swept up the rubbish with his beard.
Jutka was scared: "Oh God, help me, what an ugly beast, what an ugly little man!"
But the dwarf spoke up:
"Good evening, Ashy Jutka!
I know what your trouble is.
Don't worry a bit, in one week I will spin every last thread
of the hemp that is here, and even wind it on the reel.
But then you must come with me."
"How can I go with you," said the girl, "when the prince has chosen me for himself?"
"Very well," said the dwarf, "I will not take you away if,
by the time I finish the spinning, you guess my name."
The girl thought: so be it.
It made no difference now which way her fate would turn.
She shook hands with the dwarf, and the bargain was made.
After that the dwarf came to the granary every night,
and he spun so fast that Jutka's eyes and mouth stood wide open in wonder.
What he spun by night he took away, and by day he reeled it in the forest branches.
When there was only one day left of the month,
the little serving boy came with supper, and Jutka asked:
"So what news is there outside, little serving boy?"
"Well, the news is that if you spin the hemp by tomorrow evening,
you will be the prince's wife."
"And didn't you hear anything else, little serving boy?"
"Yes, I did.
This afternoon I went hunting with the prince,
and as we wandered in the forest, we heard a clattering among the branches.
We looked up, and what did we see there?
A teeny-tiny dwarf with a beard seven yards long, just imagine!
He was reeling among the branches, and he kept saying:
I am Tirpe-Torpe Gyurka,
My wife will be Ashy Jutka.
The prince laughed loudly
at what that ugly little man was saying, and with that we went on."
Oh, how glad Ashy Jutka was to hear this!
Now she knew the dwarf's name.
The hemp would be spun, and still she would not have to go with the dwarf.
On the last evening the dwarf came and said to the girl:
"Now, Jutka, I have spun the hemp to the last thread, now come with me.
Or do you perhaps know my name?"
"Of course I know it," said Jutka, "your name is Tirpe-Torpe Gyurka."
In the morning came the prince, and the whole court with him.
Oh, how amazed they all were!
Everyone said that since the world began, no human eye had seen such a thing.
Even the old king said:
"Well, my son, until now I was against your marriage,
but now I say: only the spade, the hoe and the great bell shall part you two."
They held the wedding right away.
And what a wedding it was!
Everyone was there who was not late.
Everyone ate and drank who got something.
Two old women especially pushed about in vain, everything was eaten up before them.
So they went off to the prince to complain.
But even the prince had never seen two such ugly women.
One's eyelids, and the other's lips, hung down to the ground.
He asked them one after the other:
"Now why have your eyelids drooped down to the ground?"
"Because, my royal lord, I spun all my life,
and my eyes were always on the spindle."
"And why have your lips drooped down?"
he asked the other.
"That is because I licked the hemp a lot, so that I could spin more."
Oh, how frightened the prince was!
Why, then even his lovely wife might grow ugly like that.
So at once he forbade Jutka
ever again in her life even to hold a spindle in her hand.
And Jutka, believe it or not, obeyed, and she lives still, if she has not died.
The Golden Thread
Once upon a time there was a poor miller who had a beautiful daughter.
Where he went, which way he went, I do not know; enough that he met the king,
and the king spoke with him, asking who he was and how he was getting on.
Who knows what the miller was thinking? Surely he wanted the king to think more of him,
for he began to boast that he had a beautiful daughter,
as lovely as the shining star in the sky, but that was nothing,
for his daughter was the kind of girl who could spin straw into gold.
"Well," said the king, "I have never heard of such a thing in all my life.
Listen, miller, if your daughter is truly so clever,
bring her to my palace tomorrow, and let me see if your words are true."
The miller's lip drooped a little, for the girl was beautiful, that much
was true, but that she could spin straw into gold was a downright lie.
But he had said it, he could not take it back, and the next day he took her to the king.
He did not say a word to his daughter, he only led her into the palace,
then left her in God's care and ran out of the palace.
The girl went in to the king and greeted him politely,
the king received her, then without a word he led her into a room.
That room was full of straw, and the king said to the girl:
"Here is the straw.
Here is the spinning wheel.
If you do not spin this straw into gold by morning, you shall die a dreadful death."
The poor girl could not even open her mouth before the king locked the door on her.
Oh dear God, the girl wept, full of worry and sorrow, for what was she to do now?
She could hardly even spin, let alone spin gold out of straw.
As she sat there crying to herself, all at once the door opened,
and in came a tiny old little man, who said:
"Good evening to you, miller's pretty daughter!
Why are you crying so bitterly?"
"How could I not cry, my dear little man, when the king has ordered me
to spin all this straw into gold!"
"What will you give me if I spin it?" asked the little man.
"I will give you my red coral beads," said the girl.
The little man took the beads, then sat down at the spinning wheel; it whirred
and turned, and with every three turns a spool was full of golden thread.
Dawn had hardly broken, and not one stalk of straw was left:
all of it had turned into shining golden thread,
and by the time the king came in, there was no sign of the little man at all.
The king was amazed, and he thought to himself: if this girl is so clever,
let her spin even more, and he led her into another chamber.
That one was full of straw too, and he told the girl
to spin it all by morning, if she loved her life.
Then he locked the door, and the girl wept to herself,
but not for long, for the door opened, the little man came in and said:
"What will you give me if I spin this straw too?"
"I will give you my gold ring, my dear little man!"
The little man took the ring and by morning he had spun every last stalk of straw:
the whole chamber shone with golden thread.
In came the king, amazed and astonished, and said to the girl:
"Now, girl, come with me to the third chamber.
It is full of straw too, and if you spin it into gold, I will make you my wife!"
He led the girl into the third chamber,
locked the door on her, and the girl just wept and wailed bitterly.
But the door opened, the tiny old man came in and asked:
"What will you give me if I spin this too?"
"I have nothing left, my dear little man!" wailed the girl.
"Then promise me that when you are queen, you will give me your first child."
The girl thought: who knows if that will ever happen; whatever will be,
will be. So she promised what the little man wished,
and he spun the straw by morning:
the king was nearly blinded by the dazzling shine when he came in that morning.
The king did not go back on his word,
he married the miller's daughter, and when a year had passed,
a lovely, beautiful child was born to the miller's daughter who had become queen.
She hardly thought of the little man, but he thought of her, and that very day he came:
"Here I am, queen!
Give me what you promised!"
Oh, how frightened the queen was! She promised him anything, a sea of treasure,
if only he would not ask for her child, but the little man said:
"I do not want your sea of treasure, I want the child."
The queen wept so hard that the whole palace rang with it,
and the little man felt sorry for her and said:
"Very well!
I will give you three days. If in that time you find out
what my name is, you may keep your child."
With that the little man went away,
and from that hour the queen racked her brains, over and over,
wondering what the little man's name could be.
She thought up all sorts of names, every which way,
and she also sent messengers all over the country
to gather every name they heard, for surely the little man's name would be among them.
The next day the little man came, and the queen said a great heap of names,
she said a hundred of them, but the little man just shook his head.
On the second day, when the little man came, the queen listed the strangest,
rarest names she could find, but she could list all she liked:
not one of them was the little man's name.
On the third day the messengers came back, but not one brought a new name.
But just as evening was falling and the sun was setting,
a weary young servant boy came and told the queen this:
"My queen, Your Majesty, I have not heard a new name either,
but as I came through the forest, I saw a little house;
in front of the house a fire was burning, and around the fire danced
and hopped a funny little man, who kept shouting:
Paul knows well what he hoes and what he mows,
My name is Riki-Roki-Rokka Paul, Rokka Paul.
Tomorrow, tomorrow, the day after, oh what fun,
The king's own son, I swear it, will be mine, will be mine!"
Oh, how glad the queen was when she heard this!
Why, that was her own little man!
Hardly a minute or two had passed when the little man came, full of confidence:
"Well, queen, do you know my name?"
The queen pretended not to know, and she tried out the strange name bit by bit:
"Riki, is it?"
"No, no!"
"Roki, is it?"
"No, no!"
"Well then, it is Riki-Roki-Rokka Paul, is it not?"
"The devil told you that, no one else!" the little man stamped in his rage.
He ran out of the palace and in his rage stamped down so hard he sank to his waist,
then he jumped out again, turned a somersault over his head,
and ran away so fast that no human eye ever saw him again.
If Riki-Roki-Rokka Paul had not run away, my tale would have lasted longer too.
The Musicians
Once upon a time there was a man who had a donkey.
The donkey was old, and since he was of little use because of his age,
his master begrudged him even the thistles, and kept thinking how to get rid of him.
Though a donkey is a donkey,
he saw what his master meant to do and thought: I will run off before I am clubbed.
For oh, people are ungrateful, they are capable even of that!
Well, he did not think about it for long,
he said goodbye to the gatepost and set off. And where did he set off to?
Why, he set off straight for Brasso.
Well, why there?
Why?
Believe it or not, he had made up his mind to become a musician there.
He knew about that too, of course he did!
On and on went the donkey, and on the way he met a hound.
This hound was old too; he lay by the roadside sighing to himself:
oh, how old I have grown, oh, how weak I have become!
In the old days, when I could run well, what a good life I had!
The donkey stopped and asked:
"Why are you sighing, why are you grieving, my friend the hound?"
"How could I not sigh, how could I not grieve, when I am old and cannot run!
My master has already passed sentence on me: he will shoot me, for I am no use to him."
"Well now, if your master wants to shoot you, come with me.
I am going to Brasso to become a musician there; you can become one too.
You have a good voice, and surely you know how to play the drum as well,
you will see what a grand life you will have.
I will blow the trumpet, you will beat the drum: what fine music that will be!"
"There is sense in what you say, you have a clever tongue,"
said the hound, and he joined the donkey: off he went with him to Brasso.
They had not gone even half an hour when they met an old cat.
The poor thing was staggering by the roadside, as gloomy as three days of rain.
"And what is wrong with you, old whisker knight?"
asked the donkey.
"Oh, do not even ask," answered the cat.
"I have grown old, my teeth have fallen out,
I cannot catch mice, and my mistress wants to drown me.
Is this what I deserve?
Oh, how she petted me when I caught mice by the hundred!"
"Never you mind," said the donkey.
"Come along with us, come to Brasso to be a musician.
You know all about night music anyway,
you will have a life there like you have never had in all your days."
The cat did not think for a single minute; he shook hands with the donkey,
joined them, and now the three of them went on toward Brasso.
