On and on they went, further and further,
then they came to a village, and there all at once they saw an old rooster
huddled sadly on top of a gate.
His head hung down, his wings drooped: anyone who saw him felt sorry for him.
"Good day to you, knight of the spurs!
And what is wrong with you?
My, how low you have fallen!"
"How could I not, my dear brother donkey,
when my mistress expects guests tomorrow and wants to feed them my old flesh."
"Oh, you silly thing," said the donkey, "surely you will not let them kill you.
Come with us to Brasso, join our band.
You have a lovely voice: you are just the one we were missing!"
Hop! The rooster fluttered down from the gate,
crowed a great crow, and marched off proudly with the band.
On and on they went, and by evening they came to a forest.
There they made camp at once: the donkey and the hound lay down under a big tree,
the cat and the rooster went up the tree, right to the top of it.
But before they fell asleep,
the rooster looked around, and not far away he caught sight of a firelight.
At once he called to his friends:
"Listen, I see a firelight not far from here, there must be a house there."
Said the donkey:
"Well then, let us get up and go there, for this is no comfortable place to sleep."
They did not think for long; they got themselves together and went toward the light.
As they went, the firelight grew bigger
and bigger, and all at once they were standing in front of the house.
It was a robbers' house!
The donkey, as the biggest of the band, went straight to the window and looked in.
"Well, what do you see, old donkey?"
asked the rooster.
"Oh my, oh my! A table all laid, with food and drink on it, and so much of it!
Around the table sit robbers, eating, drinking, having a merry time."
"How good it would be if we could sit down at the table too," said the rooster.
"I believe you," agreed the donkey.
All of them put their heads together and talked it over,
how they could chase the robbers away.
And since they were all very clever, the talking did not last long.
Just listen to what they did.
The donkey put his two front hooves up on the window ledge,
the dog jumped up onto the donkey's back,
the cat onto the dog, and the rooster onto the very top of the cat's head.
When they were nicely settled like this, all at once they began to make music:
the donkey brayed, the dog barked,
the cat meowed, the rooster crowed,
and to this merry music they broke the window, and whoosh, into the house!
Oh, Holy Mary, Saint Joseph! How frightened the robbers were!
They thought ghosts were about,
so up they jumped from the table and ran head over heels out into the forest.
That was just what the musicians wanted; they sat down at the table, ate, drank,
played music, and grew so merry that they nearly kicked out the side of the house.
Toward midnight they grew sleepy, put out the fire and lay down.
The donkey went out into the farmyard and lay down at the foot of a haystack,
the hound stretched out behind the door,
the cat lay down on the hearth, and the rooster flew up onto the perch.
In a minute or two they were sleeping like logs, but the robbers were not sleeping:
from far off they watched in great fright to see what was happening in their house.
Then all at once they saw the firelight go out,
and the house went dark, and they thought: perhaps the ghosts have gone.
"Go and look," said the leader to one of them, "and let us see if they have gone."
The robber went off, groped his way into the room, and went straight to the hearth,
because he saw embers glowing there.
Ah, but it was the cat's eyes.
The robber did not know that, how could he have known?
He held a match to the cat's eyes.
Well, he could hold it there, the match did not light, but something else happened!
The cat leapt at the robber's face, hissed at him and scratched him all over.
Oh, how frightened the robber was! He ran off out of his wits,
but as he ran out through the door, the dog bit him in the leg,
and as he ran across the yard howling terribly,
the donkey by the haystack gave him a mighty kick in the side.
Only the rooster did not hurt him: he woke at the noise and shouted with all his might:
cock-a-doodle-doo, cock-a-doodle-dee! and he flapped his wings.
The robber ran on out of his wits and could hardly tell what had happened to him.
"Oh, oh, let us run as far as our eyes can see, we cannot stay here.
On the hearth sits an old witch.
When I tried to light a fire, she blew in my eyes and scratched my face all over;
by the door stood a man, and he stabbed me in the leg with a big knife;
I ran into the yard, past the haystack,
and there some black monster struck me in the side with a club,
so hard that I will be a beggar from it all my life.
On the roof of the house sits the judge, and he kept shouting:
bring the robber here, bring him here!"
Well, the robbers never dared even to look toward the house again; they ran
as if they had vanished from sight,
and the musicians stayed on in the house and lived merrily for as long as they had food.
And they are living still, if they have not died.
The King's Hares
Once upon a time, beyond the seven times seven lands,
there lived a poor woman, and she had three sons.
They were as poor as church mice; they cooked with water
and stirred it with a stick, and lived from one day to the next.
The lads grew tired of this hard life, and they made up their minds
that they would go out from home somewhere,
for they could not go on like this forever and a day.
One day the eldest said to his mother:
"Mother dear, bake me a cake in the ashes,
for I am setting out to try my luck."
The poor woman baked it, and the lad set out into the wide world.
On and on he went, over hills and valleys, and came to a golden well.
He sat down beside it, took out his ash cake, and began to eat.
As he sat there eating, a little mouse ran up to him and said:
"Listen, lad, give me a bite of that cake,
for it is seven whole days since I have eaten a single bite."
"I don't care," said the lad,
"even if you have not eaten for seventy-seven days, as long as I have enough."
The little mouse crept away very sadly
and hid in a hole, and the lad went on his way.
He went and went until he came to the king's city.
He went straight to the palace, sat down by the gate, and waited for good luck.
Then all at once the king himself came out,
saw the lad, even greeted him, and asked:
"What brings you here, poor lad?"
"Your Majesty, I put my life and death in your hands;
I am looking for work, if I can find any."
The king said:
"Come in, lad. I have a hundred hares in my yard, and I give them to you.
Drive them out to the meadow, but guard them so well
that not one gets lost, or else it is the hares and your head!"
Next morning the lad drove the hundred hares out,
but as soon as they reached the meadow, the hundred ran a hundred ways.
Oh, how the lad lost heart! He did not even dare look toward the palace;
he ran away and did not stop until he got home.
At home he told where he had been and all that had happened to him.
Then the second lad stepped forward
to try his luck, and he spat on his hands hard,
saying he would guard those hundred hares, heaven knows, if it took his life.
But he did just as "well" as the eldest.
At the golden well he too sat down to eat,
and the mouse asked him too for a bite of the ash cake, but he gave it none.
Then he went on to the king's city and took service with the king,
but the first morning he drove the hares out, the hundred ran a hundred ways.
He too went home very sadly, and now the youngest lad got ready to go:
perhaps luck would be kinder to him.
His mother baked him an ash cake as big
as a big cart wheel, and with it he set out into the world.
On and on he went, and came to the golden well.
As he sat there eating, the mouse ran up and asked him very nicely
to give it, for heaven's sake, a bite of cake,
for it was fourteen whole days since it had eaten.
"Gladly, little mouse," said the lad,
"perhaps the good Lord will help me, so I won't have to live long on this cake."
The little mouse thanked him kindly and said:
"Well, poor lad, a good deed brings a good deed back!
I asked your two brothers, neither gave me anything, and the Lord helped neither."
With that it ran into its hole and came back with a little horn.
"I give you this horn," said the mouse. "Keep it, it may be useful."
"Why, what could I ever do with this?"
asked the lad.
"Just take it," said the mouse, "and whatever danger you are in,
blow it, and all that is bad will turn to good."
"Well," thought the poor lad,
"if it does no good, it does no harm. I'll take it with me."
He put it in his bag, went on, and did not stop until the king's city,
and in it, until the gate of the king's palace.
He arrived, sat down in the gateway, and soon the king came by.
"What are you looking for here, poor lad?"
asked the king.
The lad told him what he wanted: to find work in some good place.
"You have come to the right place," said the king. "I have a hundred hares,
and they need a clever herder, for I have not found one I like yet."
They shook hands at once, but the king warned the lad most strictly
that not one hare must be lost, or else it would be the hares and his head!
Very well.
Next morning the lad went out to the meadow with the hundred hares,
but before they even sniffed the grass, they ran off every which way.
"Oh, Holy Mary, Saint Joseph!" cried the lad. "What shall I do now?"
Then he remembered the horn; he pulled it out and blew it,
and the hundred hares turned at once and ran together like so many sheep.
The king saw this from the porch of the palace;
he shook his head and could not for the life of him think
what devilish trick the lad had used to gather those hares.
"Just wait," he thought, "today at least one of the hundred will be missing!
If not, I will put you to another test."
At once he ordered a servant girl to go out to the meadow with a sack
and ask the herder for a hare in the king's name.
The girl went out and asked for the hare, but the lad said
he would not give one even for heaven's sake, for his head was dear to him.
"But this and that," said the girl, "there is a feast at the house,
and the king will have both our heads off if there is no hare on the table."
As they argued like this, from who knows where
the little mouse appeared and whispered to the lad:
"Just give her one, don't be afraid, and leave the rest to me!"
The lad listened to the mouse, quickly grabbed a hare by the ears,
put it in the sack, and the girl set off with it.
That very minute the little mouse jumped up onto the sack,
and before the girl had taken a hundred steps, it chewed open the end of the sack;
the hare jumped out and ran back to the others as fast as it could go.
The mouse jumped down from the sack,
quickly picked up a big lump of cow dung and pushed it into the sack instead.
In the evening the lad went home and drove the hundred hares in at the big gate.
Out came the king to meet him, cursing so that the whole yard shook.
"Come here, come here, you good-for-nothing! What did you send me in that sack?"
The lad answered:
"May God not be my God if it was not a hare, Your Majesty."
They called the servant girl.
"Well, girl, what did the herder give you?"
"Truly, Your Majesty,
I put my life and death in your hands, he really gave me a hare."
"Hm," said the king,
"I never ate anything like that in all my life. So where is the hare now?"
They counted the hares once, twice, three times, but it always came to a hundred.
"Well, listen, poor lad," said the king,
"I never had a herder like you, who sends a hare and still has none missing.
So what do you wish for?"
"Only a tub of money, Your Majesty, for we are very poor at home."
At once the king had a great big sack of money measured out,
so big that the lad needed twelve oxen to pull it home.
And they became so very rich that people came from far lands to marvel at them.
They are still alive today, if they have not died.
The Steel Ring
Once upon a time there was a poor man.
One day this poor man went into the forest for wood.
As he was picking up dry branches, he picked up a little snake with them.
He wanted to kill it, but the little snake spoke up and said:
"Don't kill me, poor man,
for I will make you happy all your life if you spare my life."
"Come now, what are you saying, little snake?" said the poor man.
"I am not such a silly fool as to believe your promise."
"Oh, but do believe me, poor man, and you will not be sorry.
Here, I give you a steel ring. Put it on your finger,
and if you ever have a wish in your life,
just turn this ring around on your finger,
and I will be there at once and grant your wish."
"So be it," thought the poor man. "If it does no good,
it does no harm." He took the ring, put it on his finger, and went home.
He had hardly settled down at home
when he turned the ring on his finger, and there was the little snake.
"What is your command, dear master?"
"My command is this," said the poor man,
"by tomorrow morning, make me a palace here
such as not even the Turkish emperor has."
"It shall be done, dear master," said the little snake,
and it vanished as if the earth had swallowed it.
Well, that evening the poor man went to bed and slept like a log.
When he woke in the morning, his eyes and mouth fell wide open,
for a shining palace had risen in place of his ragged little hut.
It was such as no human eye had ever seen in this world!
Everything around was pure gold, every single thing.
Even the table was gold,
and in its middle stood a dish of pure gold as big as a cart wheel.
"Well," said the poor man to himself, "that little snake did not trick me after all.
My, how wise I was to spare its life!"
Again he turned the ring, and that very moment the little snake was there.
"What is your command, dear master?"
"My command is that you bring me the Black King's daughter to be my wife."
"It shall be done, dear master!"
And as true as I live,
the next morning the Black King's daughter was there with him in a room.
And listen, she was such a wonderfully beautiful girl
that you could look at the sun, but not at her.
Oh, the poor man was happy; he lived like an emperor.
He got everything his heart desired;
he only had to give that steel ring one twist,
and the little snake was there and brought him everything.
A long, long time passed, and one day the poor man went out of that lovely palace.
He left home and forgot the steel ring there.
Just then an old junk dealer went past the palace, shouting at the top of his voice:
"Rings for sale!
Rings!"
The wife looked out and called him in,
and the poor thing gave him the steel ring for a gold ring, and paid extra too.
But somehow or other, the junk dealer knew the secret of the steel ring,
and as soon as he was out in the street, he turned it once.
That very moment the little snake was there.
It asked:
"What is your command, dear master?"
"My command is that you lift up this palace, with the wife
and everything in it, and take it beyond the Operencian Sea."
"It shall be done, dear master!"
Oh dear good Lord, by the time the poor man came home,
only the empty ground was left of that dear, lovely, shining palace!
Ah! He grew very sad and set out into the world in sorrow,
hoping he might find his palace somewhere.
On and on he went, over hills and valleys, past the seven times seven lands.
As he reached the near shore of the Operencian Sea,
he saw a dog lying half dead, rolling about on the seashore.
It whimpered and whined bitterly and begged the poor man with dreadful howling
to heal it and not leave it there to die.
The poor man gathered all sorts of good herbs,
healed it with them, and the two went on together.
They had gone barely a good gunshot away when they found a sick cat.
It too begged the poor man to heal it.
Very well, he healed it, and now the three of them went on.
On and on they went along the seashore, and suddenly the poor man cried out:
"Look, look there!
My palace is over on the far shore.
Well, somebody has moved that nicely!
Oh!
Oh!
Lord Jesus Christ, if by some wonder I could get across,
I would not take a mare with her foal for it."
The dog said:
"Don't be sad, poor man!
You did me good, and a good deed brings a good deed back.
I will swim across the sea and think of something."
The cat said that it too would go across with the dog, even if it cost its life,
and would not close its eyes until the palace was back in its old place.
They did not take long to get ready: the dog jumped quickly into the sea,
the cat after it, climbed onto the dog's back, and so they swam across.
But so I don't get my words mixed up: the poor man told the dog clearly,
and the cat too, that there must be a steel ring in that palace.
They must get hold of it no matter what, and pay no heed to anything else.
Once they had the ring, they should hurry back, and the rest was his worry.
They swam across and went into the palace.
There lay the junk dealer asleep, with the ring tied to his beard.
That was all the cat needed.
It crept up to the bed, gently untied the ring, and then off they went,
as fast as they could! They ran out of the palace,
into the sea, and swam back very quickly.
But just when they reached the very middle of the sea, now listen
to what that wretched "frog-cat" of a cat did!
A fish swam by, the cat snapped at it, and dropped the ring into the sea.
Oh my goodness, what a to-do there was!
The dog wanted to drown the foolish cat in the sea,
but the cat begged so hard that the dog spared its life after all.
Well, what were they to do now, which way were they to turn?
They grieved terribly; they did not dare swim back without the ring.
They had to find it, even if it was at the bottom of the earth.
As they grieved like this, the cat caught a fish.
And this was the son of the king of the fishes!
The little fish begged:
"Don't kill me, dear cat, I am the son of the fish king;
you will not be sorry if you spare my life!"
They took it to the king of the fishes and told him what had happened.
They would spare his son's life if he found that ring,
for surely one of the fish had swallowed it.
The king of the fishes at once called a great meeting and asked every fish
whether it had a ring, but each one only answered
that none of its family had ever had a ring.
The dog grew very sad, and so did the cat,
and they were just about to leave when word came that one fish was still away.
They waited a little; perhaps that one had the ring.
And sure enough, a "lame" fish came, all in a sweat, and it brought the ring!
Oh, how glad the dog was, and the cat too!
The cat wanted to grab the ring, but the dog growled loudly:
"Leave it, you! I won't trust you with it again!
You just curl up on my back, and I will take the ring in my mouth!"
They did not even say "bless you", they ran off so fast.
They swam out to the shore and handed the ring to the poor man.
At once he put it on his finger, gave it a twist, and the little snake was there.
"What is your command, dear master?"
"My command is this," said the poor man,
"take that house back to its old place, and leave the junk dealer on the far shore."
"It shall be done, dear master."
And it all happened as the poor man commanded.
The lovely palace came back, with the wife and everything in it,
to where it had first stood, and the poor man lived happily again.
He did not forget the dog and the cat either:
he bathed them in milk and butter, and gave them a log for a rub now and then.
It is true that ever since then they have been angry with each other,
but they are still alive, if they have not died.
The Fisherman and His Wife
Once upon a time there was a fisherman and his wife.
They lived in a little hut by the sea,
and they were very poor, for some days a fish took the hook and some days none did.
Well, what happened one day?
What happened was that a terribly big shark got caught on the fisherman's hook.
The fisherman pulled and pulled, but the fish spoke:
"Spare my life! I am not a fish, I am an enchanted prince.
What good would I be to you if you caught me?
You could not eat my flesh anyway."
"You are right," said the fisherman. "Go with God, if you are truly not a real fish."
He let the fish go and went home with an empty bag.
"Well now, did you catch no fish again?"
asked his wife.
"What will become of us?"
"Oh, I did catch one," said the fisherman,
"I caught a terribly big shark, but it was not a real fish.
It said it was an enchanted prince, and it begged until I let it go."
"Well, that was a foolish thing to do.
You should not have let it go until it granted you a wish."
"And what would I have wished for?"
"Why, that it build us a proper house instead of this miserable hut.
Go right back, and if it gets caught on your hook once more,
do not let it go until it promises the house."
The fisherman only shook his head, for he thought it was a useless wish,
but he went back to the seashore and began to call:
"Are you there, are you there,
Enchanted prince of the sea?
Do you hear, do you hear?
Come up from the sea to me."
At that very moment the sea gave a great splash,
it sloshed, and up popped the fish and asked the fisherman:
"What do you want, old fisherman?"
The fisherman answered:
"A house is better than a hut.
This is what my wife would like:
A house to live in, not a hut."
Said the fish:
"Go on home, old fisherman,
By morning the house will stand."
And sure enough, by morning a pretty little stone house stood there; they woke in it.
"There, you see," said the wife, "you only have to wish for something and it comes true.
Now go back and tell it that a pretty little stone house
is nice, very nice, but too small for us; it should build a palace instead."
"Oh, wife, wife, what are you thinking?
This house is big enough for us.
What would you do in a palace?"
"Never you mind that, just go and ask for a palace!"
"The fish will be angry, wife, do not be silly!"
"Angry or not, just say what I tell you.
By tomorrow morning there must be a palace here, one as fine as the king's."
What could he do? The fisherman went and called the fish:
"Are you there, are you there,
Enchanted prince of the sea?
Do you hear, do you hear?
Come up from the sea to me."
The fish came at once and asked:
"What do you want, old fisherman?"
The fisherman answered:
"That house is too small for us.
This is what my wife would like:
A palace all her own to live in."
Said the fish:
"Then go on home, nice and slow,
In the morning the palace will be ready."
The fisherman went home, they went to bed, and in the morning they woke in a palace,
a palace so huge that it had seventy-seven rooms,
and in the rooms were golden benches, tables, beds, and mirrors down to the floor.
Even the windows were pure gold, and so were the stairs.
Everywhere footmen and maids were bustling about;
not far from the palace stood a great big stable, full of horses with golden coats:
just as the fisherman and his wife stepped inside,
the grooms were combing them with golden combs and brushing them with golden brushes.
"Well," said the wife, "was it not a good thing that I wished for a palace?"
"Good, good," said the fisherman, "now you cannot wish for anything more."
"I will still think about that," said the wife.
The next morning the wife said:
"This palace is fine, very fine, but it would only be truly fine if I were king.
Go to the fish and tell it that I want to be king."
"Wife, wife, what are you saying?
I do not even dare to say that!"
"Why would you not dare?
Just go and tell it boldly that I want to be king."
The fisherman went off very sadly, for he did not like his wife's doings at all.
Now the enchanted prince would surely be angry, and how could he not be!
And indeed, the sea was not clear as at other times, it was grey,
it was dirty, as if it were angry too, and it roared and growled loudly.
But he feared his wife even more than the sea, more
than the enchanted prince, so he called out as before:
"Are you there, are you there,
Enchanted prince of the sea?
Do you hear, do you hear?
Come up from the sea to me!"
The sea gave a great slosh and splash, the fish popped up and asked the fisherman:
"What is wrong, what is wrong, old fisherman?
Is the house perhaps not big enough?"
The fisherman answered:
"Oh, it is big enough, there is nothing wrong, nothing,
Only my wife wants to be king!"
Said the fish:
"If that is all she wishes for,
Then she shall be king, for sure!"
Well, good Lord, by the time the fisherman got home, the palace had grown bigger,
and the yard too; guards stood in front of the palace,
generals walked up and down in the yard,
the army band played its music, the soldiers marched,
turning right, turning left,
and the fisherman's wife sat in the palace's biggest hall on a throne of pure gold,
guards stood before her, coming and going,
and the people of the court ran about and bowed before her.
"Oh, my Lord!" The fisherman clapped his hands. "So you have really become king?"
"King indeed," said the wife.
"Can you not see?
Here is the crown on my head."
"Well, that is truly a fine thing.
With this you can be content until your dying day."
"You might be content, but not I.
Go back to the fish at once and tell it that I want to be pope."
"Oh wife, wife, what are you saying?
There is only one pope in the whole world, you cannot be that."
"Not another word!" the wife cried out,
"Off with you, or I will have your head cut off at once!"
The poor fisherman shivered all over at this terribly big wish.
But it was no use; still he went to the seashore and spoke to the fish:
"Are you there, are you there,
Enchanted prince of the sea?
Do you hear, do you hear?
Come up from the sea to me."
Oh, but the sea was murky, so very murky, and it roared
and rumbled so that the poor fisherman covered his eyes and ears in fright.
Then all at once the fish leapt up, and you could see that it was angry now too.
It shouted at the fisherman:
"Well, what do you want? Come here and tell,
Is being king not enough as well?"
The fisherman answered:
"Oh, it is not enough, not enough,
Now she would like to be pope!"
"Only pope?"
said the shark,
"So be it, let her be pope!"
The fisherman ran home full of joy,
and by the royal palace stood a church so big that its towers (there were a thousand!)
nearly touched the sky. He went in, and there sat his wife on her throne,
kindly giving her blessing to the people, and all who could get near kissed her feet.
So the fisherman pushed his way up too, fell on his knees,
and kissed his wife's feet, and said as he did so:
"Well, wife, now you have become pope as well,
you cannot be more than this, so now you can truly be content."
"We shall see," said the wife.
All night she did not sleep, she kept tossing and turning,
and kept thinking about what else she could become.
"Aha, I have it!"
cried the wife.
"I will become God."
She woke her husband and told him to run to the fish at once
and tell it her wish: she wanted to be God, being pope was not enough for her.
"Wife, wife, you have lost your mind! What are you thinking?"
"What I am thinking is my business. Go, and be quick."
Oh, dear good God, the poor fisherman shivered twice before he reached the sea.
And even more when he saw the sea!
For whatever it had been before, now the sea roared and bellowed,
it swirled and tossed as if it wanted to swallow the whole world.
The poor fisherman just stood in one place and did not even dare to open his mouth.
But the fish came, it did not wait for a question, it asked in a terrible rage:
"Is being pope not enough?
What more could she want now?"
The fisherman answered, trembling, his teeth chattering:
"Oh dear, what can I do?
Now she wants to be God!"
Oh, the enchanted prince flew into a terrible rage,
his eyes threw sparks, and he roared so loud the poor fisherman fell over in fright.
"What does the silly old goose want?
Back to the hut with her, go!"
At that very moment the sea covered everything, simply everything,
and the next morning, when it had gone back into its bed,
there was nothing on the seashore but the little hut,
and in front of it sat the fisherman and his wife, very sad, just like before.
They are still alive today, if they have not died.
Lucky John
Once upon a time there was a lad, and his name was John.
This John lived with a farmer for seven whole years,
and when the seventh year was over, he said to his master:
"Master, my time is up, now I am going home to my dear mother: please pay me my wages."
"Very well, John," said the farmer,
"you have been a good lad, you served me honestly, here are your wages."
He gave him a lump of gold as big
as John's head, and even a little bigger than that.
John tied it up in a sack, put it on his shoulder and set off for home.
As he walked along, a man on horseback came toward him, and John began to sigh:
"Oh my, what a fine thing riding is!
The rider sits on his horse just like on a chair, he does not stumble on the stones,
he does not wear out his boots, and still he moves along."
The rider heard this and said to John:
"Well then, why do you go on foot?"
"Because," said John, "I have no horse.
And I must carry this gold home: I served seven years for it!
Oh, but it is heavy, my shoulder is about to break."
"Do you know what?
Let us trade," said the rider.
"I will give you the horse, and you give me the gold."
"Gladly," said John, and in that very moment he threw the sack off his shoulder.
The rider got off the horse, helped John up onto it, and even gave him good advice:
"Now, if you want to go fast, just urge it on:
gee up, gee up! and it will run like the swift wind."
Well, they wished each other God's blessing, parted, and went their two ways.
Oh, how happy John was!
Now he had a horse.
And what a horse!
He tugged at the reins and urged the horse on: gee up,
gee up! and the horse really did dash off, so fast
that John tipped now to the left, now to the right, and he tipped this way
and that, until all at once, bump! he tumbled into the ditch.
The poor fellow could hardly scramble up, his bones creaked,
every limb ached, and he was very sorry he had traded the gold for a horse.
Just as he got up, a man came along that way, driving a cow.
This man caught the horse and asked John:
"What is wrong, little brother?
The horse threw you off, did it not?"
"Oh, it did, may the wolves eat it!
Well, I will never sit on this nasty beast again.
Oh, a cow is so much better than a horse!
You can stroll quietly behind it, and it gives you milk and butter too."
"Do you know what," said the farmer, "let us trade."
"Gladly," said John.
"Better your neck gets broken than mine!"
"Do not you worry about that," said the farmer,
and with that he jumped onto the horse and galloped off like the swift wind.
John set off with the cow too, and they ambled along nice and slowly.
Oh my, how happy John was!
Now he would have no worries for the rest of his life.
If he had bread, he would have milk and butter, and cheese if he liked: what more, John?
On the way he stopped at an inn, and there he ate
what bread he had with him; he had a few pennies, so he drank some wine too,
then in a merry mood he set off again, and the two of them walked on,
they walked and walked, ambling slowly toward home.
It was getting near noon, and the heat was stifling,
and John grew so faint with thirst that his tongue hung out.
He thought to himself: here is the cow, I will milk it and my thirst will be gone.
He tied the cow to a tree, and since he had no pail with him (where would he get one?),
he took his cap, held it under the cow's udder and began to milk.
He milked and milked, but not a single drop of milk came out.
And because he wanted milk no matter what, he squeezed and tugged hard at the udder,
the cow grew tired of the joke and kicked John in the head so hard
that he fell flat on his back, lay sprawled out, and even fainted, the poor lad.
When at long last he woke up, he did not know where he was: in the sky or on the ground.
Luckily, a butcher came along that way, pushing a piglet in his wheelbarrow.
He stopped and asked John:
"What is wrong, little brother?"
John told him what had happened.
The butcher held out his flask and offered him a drink, to help him come round.
Then he looked at the cow, shook his head and said:
"You can milk this one all you like, little brother, there is not a drop of milk in her.
She is an old beast, she will never give milk again in all this world."
Oh, how sad John became!
"Well, who would have thought it," he grumbled to himself.
"What shall I do now?
Have her killed?
Who will eat the meat of this old beast?"
"Do you know what," said the butcher, "I will help you out of your trouble.
I will give you this piglet, and you give me the cow,
I will cut up her meat and somehow sell it with the rest of my meat."
"Oh, God bless you, sir!" John thanked him.
They took the piglet off the wheelbarrow,
tied a rope to its hind leg, and John set off with it.
He could hardly contain himself, he was bursting with joy to see
how lucky he was, what a good bargain he had made again!
So on they went, walking and walking.
All at once a young lad joined him, carrying a fine white goose under his arm.
They fell to talking; John told him of his great good luck,
and the lad told him he was taking the goose to a christening feast.
"Just lift it, feel how heavy it is," said the lad.
"No wonder, we fattened it for eight weeks.
Well, whoever eats this will be licking his lips afterwards, I know."
John took the goose in his hands and lifted it.
"It really is good and heavy," he said, "but my piglet is no small thing either!"
Meanwhile the lad looked around worriedly, shook his head and hummed.
Then at last he spoke up:
"Listen, my friend, you are going to get into trouble with this piglet."
"Why would I get into trouble?"
"Because I just heard in the village,
the one I came through, that someone stole a piglet from the mayor.
People are searching for it everywhere.
What if this is the stolen piglet?
I tell you truly, you will end up in prison."
Oh, how frightened John was!
He began to beg the lad to trade with him.
He would gladly give him the piglet for the goose, if only he could keep out of trouble.
The lad made him beg for a while, then, so be it, he gave John the goose,
and with the piglet he quickly turned onto a side road and swiftly vanished.
John went on his way too, turning the trade over in his mind.
"If I think it over well," he said to himself, "I made a good trade.
For one thing, this fat goose has plenty of fat; for another,
it has feathers too, we will stuff a pillow with them. Oh, how glad my mother will be!"
So John walked on and on, and when he reached the last village,
he saw an old knife grinder there, grinding busily and singing all the while:
"Round and round the wheel goes,
Money in my pocket grows.
I just grind the knives and shears,
Coins jingle in my pocket here!"
John stopped, greeted the grinder and said:
"Oh, you must have a good life, sir, to be in such a merry mood!"
"I should say so," answered the grinder.
"No man on earth has it better than a knife grinder.
He just grinds and grinds, and his pocket never empties, it is always full of money."
"Is that really so?"
"It is really so.
And where did you buy that fine goose?"
"I did not buy it, I traded it for a piglet."
"For a piglet?
Is that really so?"
"It is really so."
"And where did you get the piglet?"
"I got it for a cow."
"Is that really so?"
"It is really so."
"And the cow?"
"I got that for a horse."
"Is that really so?"
"It is really so."
"And the horse?"
"I got that for a lump of gold as big as my head."
"Is that really so?"
"It is really so.
I could even swear to it."
"Well, listen," said the grinder, "I have seen many lucky men,
but never one like you, and I have grown old and eaten the best of my bread."
"I should say so!"
"You see, it is a pity you are not a knife grinder.
Then you would have lots of money."
"That is true," said John, "but I have no grindstone."
"Do you know what, I will give you a grindstone.
You can make a start with that.
And you give me the goose."
"Gladly, old man!" cried John with great joy.
They shook hands on it right there, and the grinder gave him a worn,
chipped grindstone, and then picked up a big stone off the ground and gave him that too:
"Here, my son, take it,
you can hammer bent nails straight with it. Use it in good health."
Well, how happy he was!
"I truly was born lucky," John said to himself as he walked along.
But all at once he grew weary, the stone grew heavier
and heavier, he was hungry and had nothing to eat;
he was thirsty and had nothing to drink. Oh dear, oh dear,
he would not have minded at all to be rid of the stones.
By blessed luck he came to a well,
there he threw down the stones and bent over the well to drink from it.
As he bent over, somehow or other, both stones went splash into the well.
"Hooray! How good!
Oh, how good!"
John jumped up with joy.
"I do not have to lug them home, oh, how good!
Well, there has never been a man in the world as lucky as I am!"
He did not stop until he got home, he ran all the way to his dear mother.
Tomorrow let John be your guest.
